content: 美國半導體巨頭輝達（英偉達）共同創辦人黃仁勳（Jensen Huang）日前被揭發與中國籍科技業高管黃樂（Alice Huang）發生婚外情。女方被懷疑與中國情報機關有關聯，涉及美國國安疑慮，黃仁勳因此辭去CEO職務，AI股市隨之震盪。 事件亦很快從國安問題擴散至更廣的社會。美國多家主流媒體用兩人姓氏做帶有性暗示的標題，遭亞裔記者團體抗議；「中國女間諜」迷因在社群上流傳，同名者甚至需要澄清。而在法國公共新聞台節目上，嘉賓直言「整個華僑社群」都有潛力當間諜，引來中國駐法使館抗議。 據美國媒體報導，黃樂曾任新加坡AI算法公司Megaspeed高管，該公司因涉嫌走私輝達晶片正接受新加坡調查。截至11月18日，美國情報機構仍不確定黃樂是否受中國政府招募、刻意接近黃仁勳。北京強烈否認指控，稱這是對中國的「抹黑」。 11月23日路透社 報導 ，輝達已確定重新任用黃仁勳為CEO，即刻生效。但隨著事件發酵，國安疑雲與晶片貿易之外，部分國際主流媒體在報導時，以其姓氏「Huang」做雙關標題，但帶有負面或性暗示的意味，引起美國亞裔記者協會（AAJA）抗議。一宗仍未釐清的間諜疑案，如何變成對整個族群的懷疑？ 亞洲姓氏不是笑點 《經濟學人》在11月9日網頁版報導中，以「Two Huangs don't make a right」為副標題， 化用 英文俗語「Two wrongs don't make a right」（兩個錯誤不會讓事情正確）。《紐約郵報》則在報紙頭版以醒目大字 刊登 「HUANG HUANG BANG BANG」，暗示兩人的性關係；後續又用「HUANG FOR HER BUCK」（原句應為「bang for her buck）作為標題， 暗指 兩人關係涉及利益交換。 將黃仁勳姓氏用在諧音文字遊戲的媒體，還包括Washington Sun（前身為政治新聞NOTUS）的「Out with a Huang」（大意為「黃轟轟烈烈地出局」），以及同為政治媒體Politico 的「Huang out to dry」（「黃被棄之不顧」）等。 2026年11月9日，《紐約郵報》及《經濟學人》以黃仁勳姓氏「Huang」做雙關標題。網上圖片 對於以上帶有諷刺意味的表述，AAJA在11月11日以「Asian names are not punchlines」（亞洲人的名字不是笑話）為題發表聲明，點名《經濟學人》和《紐約郵報》，呼籲新聞編輯室在設計標題和報導框架時，不應以本就面臨刻板印象的群體為代價。 AAJA指出，報導間諜嫌疑是重要的新聞工作，但在涉及國家安全的報導中，將常見亞洲姓氏作為笑點，可能強化亞裔身分與間諜、犯罪之間的關聯。協會也呼籲，應在報導時區分中國政府、中國公民和亞裔美國人等概念，不以人的族裔背景或國籍判斷其政治忠誠度。 截至本稿發布，Washington Sun已修改網路版標題。該媒體發言人表示：「我們無意冒犯讀者……今後會注意避免任何無意的後果。」《經濟學人》則仍保留原有副標題。 桃色陷阱敘事，模糊了誰的責任？ 除了姓氏雙關，《紐約郵報》也在網頁版標題以「caught in Beijing's honeytrap」 形容 黃仁勳的處境，暗示他可能落入北京設下的桃色陷阱。美國商業媒體《Fast Company》評論認為，這種敘事容易將身居高位的掌權男性描繪成受到誘惑的受害者，模糊男性高管對自身行為的責任。在國安因素未釐清之前，這種表述也忽略黃樂身為科技公司高管的專業身分，僅保留性關係的面向。 爭議也映照出美國社會長期以來對亞裔政治忠誠度的懷疑。一項2025年學術研究 顯示 ，受訪者接觸與中國間諜活動有關的資訊後，對於IT、行銷產業的華裔求職者評價有所下降，但對於歷史教師等其他行業的華裔求職者印象沒有顯著改變 。 報導框架引發爭議的同時，「中國女間諜」（Chinese Spy）笑話也迅速在社群平台流傳，儘管黃仁勳後續又被揭露兩段婚外情，涉及的女性均非亞裔。比起國安疑慮，網絡討論更集中在性別與種族刻板印象。網路媒體BuzzFeed 整理 了29則不同社群平台的搞笑貼文，不少圍繞在男性能否抵擋「女間諜」的誘惑展開。 X平台上，一則 貼文 寫道：「I'm seeing a pattern here」（我看出一個規律）。文內圖片將黃仁勳與其他科技及商業界知名男性、其亞裔伴侶的照片拼貼在一起，包括Meta創辦人祖克柏（Mark Zuckerberg），以及甲骨文共同創辦人艾里森（Larry Ellison）等，貼文閱讀量迅速超過千萬。其他自媒體帳號 跟進 這個迷因，在短片中將鏡頭轉向自己的亞裔伴侶，故作懷疑地打量對方。 也有亞裔女性主動加入。加拿大亞裔創作者Leenda Dong在短影片中 模仿 一名試圖接近科技富豪竊取機密的女性，表示自己「很喜歡半導體」，一邊調情、一邊詢問電腦密碼與安全驗證問題，影片得到超過90萬按讚。 但在日常生活中，一些科技業亞裔女性已為此困擾。美國商業媒體《Business Insider》 採訪 了多位同名的 Alice Huang，其中，在德州奧斯汀求職的Alice Huang已將自己Linkedin標題改為「NOT A SPY」（不是間諜）。另一名在舊金山灣區半導體產業工作的同名女性則表示，一些多年未聯繫的老友或同事也開始傳訊息給她。她說，Alice Huang是台灣常見的英文名字。 不過，玩笑的邊界本不明確。也有同名女性表示，自己已經想好明年萬聖節的裝扮：她要扮成 Megaspeed 高階主管，丈夫則扮成 GPU，而年僅1歲的女兒將扮成穿著招牌皮夾克的黃仁勳。 2024年6月2日。英偉達執行長黃仁勳在台北國際電腦展（COMPUTEX 2024）發表主題演講後，與黃樂在場傾談。攝：Ann Wang/Reuters/達志影像 ​ 從玩笑到指控，法國電視的「華僑間諜論」 如果美國的爭議多停在玩笑與刻板印象，在法國，黃仁勳事件的後續討論則掀起一場不小的風波。 11月13日，公共新聞台Franceinfo時事評論類節目《知情者》（ Les Informés ）以黃仁勳事件為題，邀請了多位嘉賓參加辯論。節目接近尾聲時，主持人阿德里安‧貝克特（Hadrien Bect）向嘉賓發問：「我們知道法國大約有多少中國間諜嗎？」，並試圖以此問題作為節目的腳註。 其中嘉賓之一，法國國際關係與戰略研究所（IRIS）研究主任納維斯（Marie-Cécile Naves）低聲回答：「整個華僑社群都有潛力（當間諜），」演播室現場傳出笑聲。作家兼評論員克魯澤（Vincent Crouzet）更補充說：「有潛力，是的。每一個中國公民，或每一個來自中國的人，仍然與（中國共產）黨保持聯繫，並定期向其彙報。」他還宣稱，「中國情報機構在全球擁有巨額聯絡人」，並可通過設於法國的所謂秘密警察站，將「很大一部分」華僑社群成員用作線人。 由於時間所限，主持人並沒有要求兩人說明證據，最後以「一場精彩的討論」收尾。根據 IRIS官網履歷 ，納維斯的主要研究領域是美國政治、法律和社會議題；而克魯澤長期以法國對外情報總局前特工的身份頻繁現身各類媒體節目，並以自身經歷為本，撰寫過多部有關情報類的書籍。 中國使館抗議，Franceinfo為未反駁致歉 節目播出後，經濟學家比爾鮑默（Benjamin Bürbaumer）將這段對話的影響 比作 「陰謀論與排外情緒的眩暈」。一些在法華裔也指出，一旦公共電視台把「整個僑民社群」列為潛在間諜，這種懷疑便可能延伸至工作場所、求職面試和日常生活。 11月20日，中國駐法國大使館發表 正式聲明 ，稱有關「中國間諜」的籠統說法「完全沒有根據」，是帶有冷戰思維和意識形態偏見的誹謗，嚴重傷害在法華僑社群。使館要求相關媒體和個人尊重中國公民的尊嚴及聲譽，並採取措施消除影響。 同一天，Franceinfo向《南華早報》 承認 ，有關華僑社群的言論引起震驚「可以理解」，並為節目直播時沒有察覺問題和提出反駁致歉，表示今後將更加警惕，也會在當晚節目中正式聲明道歉。但需要注意的是，Franceinfo的道歉僅僅只能針對其主持人和編輯團隊沒有及時介入，不能替代兩位嘉賓的態度。上述言論涉及的兩名嘉賓——納維斯和克魯澤，目前均未回應置評請求或在個人社交平台上發佈任何說明。 此外，Franceinfo同日推出的 專題片 以《中國：新間諜大師的秘密》為題，將黃仁勳事件放進中國情報機構擴張的框架，並延伸至電動汽車、留學生和衛星設施等議題。節目介紹甚至稱，中國情報機構「處於輝達醜聞的核心」。 評論、審查與監管的邊界 克魯澤經常以「前DGSE特工」或情報專家身份出現在法國電視節目中，但他本人承認，自己沒有正式加入法國對外情報總局（DGSE），而是長期「為DGSE提供服務」。法國媒體《快報》（L’Express）在今年3月發表 調查 報道中，採訪了多名前DGSE成員，其中一些人質疑克魯澤的描述。研究法國情報機構的記者諾坦（Jean-Christophe Notin）認為，克魯澤更準確的身份是「榮譽聯絡人」（ honorable correspondant ），即利用真實職業及海外關係為DGSE提供情報，但並非正式特工。 這並不意味著克魯澤的身份為假，爭議在於他是否誇大了正式身份、所受訓練及在秘密部門的角色。DGSE曾在出版前審閱他的自傳體回憶錄，但僅限於涉及國安的內容，不能看做官方替其故事真實性背書。 然而，克魯澤的說法並非毫無依據。2017年通過的中國《國家情報法》第七條規定：「任何組織和公民都應當依法支持、協助和配合國家情報工作」，並須保守所知悉的秘密。第十四條允許情報機構要求有關機關、組織和公民提供必要協助；第十條則規定，中國情報機構可以在「境內外」開展工作。2015年《國家安全法》第七十七條也要求公民和組織及時報告危害國家安全活動的線索、如實提供所掌握的證據，並向國家安全、公安及軍事機關提供必要協助。 「歡迎來到法國」：我在法國街頭的三場遊行 法國大學生、臺裔父母的高中生、來讀預科的中國人，人生背景各不相同的人們走上街頭，他們都有怎樣的訴求？ 這些措辭寬泛的義務，確實構成歐美國家審查中國企業、科研人員及跨境數據活動的制度背景。然而，「可能被依法要求配合」不等於每名中國公民已被招募，更不能證明他們正在「定期彙報」。中國法律也不能因為血統，直接延伸至已加入法國國籍或出生於法國的華裔。克魯澤的說法恐怕跨越了從法律風險到集體指控的界線。 儘管這次爭議尚未進入司法或監管程序，但法國已有頗為相似的先例。2022年，法國最高行政法院曾經支持了監管機構對電視台CNews施以行政處罰。CNews電視台一名評論員不加區分地將無家人陪同進入法國的外籍未成年人描述為「小偷、強姦犯和殺人犯」，主持人及其他在場人士也未明確反駁。 法院當時認為，這些言論可能煽動對特定群體的仇恨和歧視，而頻道未能履行對節目內容及直播現場的控制義務，因此確認監管機構的行政處罰有合法依據。

content: 第八章 徒有虚名 一 中标 我从银行出来，档案袋里装着一份律师费二百八十万元的代理合同。这可能是我律师生涯中最大的一个案子，但我的心情和这个袋子一样沉重。 这个案子是我投标拿到的。几天前，国际会议中心三百平方米的大会议厅里聚集了五十多家律师事务所的律师，争夺某银行一个标的三个亿的大案。银行副行长和一位从法院退休的高级顾问坐在首席，每位律师有十分钟发言时间陈述方案。会议开了一整天，午饭也是在会议桌上吃的盒饭。到下午六点，所有律师都讲完了，副行长和那位顾问显然很失望。副行长收拾材料正要离开，顾问忽然说，还有一位律师没发言，听听他的意见。他指的是我。 案情简单而又复杂。一个武汉商人和葫芦岛的一家公司作为出资人，成立了阳光房地产公司，圈了二百亩土地，注册资金六百万，随后以一千二百万的价格把公司转让给当地人彭和。彭和以阳光公司的名义与三十多家建筑公司签订了建筑合同，又组织一千多户购房人与银行签订了按揭合同，案值合计超过三个亿。复杂之处在于，两个股东并不实际存在，操控此事的是胡杰和他的情人韩菊。胡杰是职业骗子，因诈骗多次入狱；韩菊曾是北京军区文工团的演员，后来进中南海当过服务员。 更复杂的是，这桩买卖只签了一纸公司买卖协议，根本没有办理股权转让手续。买卖双方是韩菊和侯新生，韩菊当时是阳光公司的法人代表，侯新生是一个汽车城的老板。侯新生加价转给彭和，彭和花点小钱到工商局办了法人代表变更，就算把企业买到了手，随后投资三千万开发房地产。眼前所有的合同都是彭和与各企业、银行和个人签订的，从法律上说全部无效。案子一旦进入司法程序，整个融资开发的合法性体系就会彻底崩溃。 我本来对这次投标没有多少信心，不是不相信自己的业务，而是不相信银行的诚意。 我曾为这家银行代理过一个三千万元的连环贷款案：三家企业互相担保，钱到手后相继关门。我调查发现，这三家企业其实是同一个人为骗贷而分别注册的。我把调查情况写进法律意见书，还跟在市公安局经侦支队的同学打了招呼，希望以刑事案件立案，查封那人在保税区的一批货物。报告送去半个月没有动静，我去问，行长说动刑事动静太大，牵涉太多，让我写份律师意见书，银行把账核销了事。 这件事让我很受刺激，主任也很生气。他去找银行理论，晚上满身酒气地回来，把一个红包扔给我，说那个案子算了，银行那帮人都拿了骗子的好处。按他的说法，如今贷款的好处费是百分之十，这种案子哪里能让我们真打。百分之十，那笔贷款的好处费就是三百万。主任扔给我的红包是一万元，算是我忙了半个月的报酬。 所以这家银行再招标，我根本不想去。主任却说一定要去，“有好事”。我半信半疑，带着助理李晓燕去了。 我一开口就说，这个案子眼下不宜走司法程序，会场顿时炸了锅。我明白同行们的心思：只有走司法程序，算出标的，律师费才有着落。我说，我们不能为了代理人的利益牺牲委托人的利益；这个案子现在进入司法程序，阳光广场就会变成烂尾楼，巨大的社会财富将付诸东流。 副行长问我有何高见。我的方案是继续履行合同：合同在经法院认定无效之前，仍然约束当事人；姑且把它们当作有效合同履行，无效合同一旦履行完毕，其成果也会得到法律的承认和保护。德恒所的一位律师追问：是否启动司法程序，并非银行或开发商一方说了算，如果阳光公司的股东起诉怎么办？合同关系这么多，任何一处起纠纷，都可能导致对整个法律基础的审查。我回答，对阳光公司的股东要先发制人，不用违约之诉，而用刑事手段压制其诉求；其他纠纷即使发生也是局部的，不会引发对公司合法性的实质审查，除非在座的人泄密。 一直没有开口的顾问不希望我再说下去，宣布散会，并重申与会律师须对今天的内容保密，银行会视情况支付保密费。行长让我把方案写成报告交给他们。我在同行们嫉妒的目光中点头。前后不过几十分钟，这个案子我拿下了。 二 水有多深 我很快领教了这个案子的分量。阳光公司和银行送来的资料足有二百公斤，我用一个月时间看完全部材料，理清了大约三千多个合同关系，做出了应对预案。 全案大致有三层法律关系。第一层是银行与阳光公司、银行与众多按揭购房人之间的关系，都是标准的合同关系，必须保证顺利履行，以保障银行资金安全。第二层是阳光公司与政府土地部门、被征地的三个村的村民、各建筑企业和供应商的关系，大体正常；但与政府的关系建立在前任股东行贿官员的基础上，非常脆弱，一旦出事，后果是毁灭性的。第三层是阳光公司内部的关系，这是全案的法律基石，也最复杂、最麻烦：所有合同都不合法，利益纠葛又十分突出，最容易出问题，也是我最头疼的部分。 当时的问题是，彭和还欠阳光公司原股东陈小光和银发房地产公司一百五十万元转让费。两个股东委派胡杰和韩菊催款，威胁说不还钱就起诉。 彭和请了海狮律师所的王雪虹律师出具法律意见书。王律师主张以转让合同无效、对方存在欺诈为由对簿公堂。单从诉讼角度看，这并没有错，但这一步一旦迈出，阳光公司的内部法律关系就要接受司法审查，合法性基石彻底崩塌，后面的所有合同都会被宣告无效，后果不堪设想。 得知消息后，我紧急约见银行的孙主管（即那位法律顾问）和彭和，坚决要求制止。我提出，我们不能只做银行的代理人，还必须成为阳光公司的代理人，因为代理目标完全实现，最大的受益者是阳光公司。彭和原是街头混混，听不懂这些，哭丧着脸说已经和王律师签了委托合同，预付了十万元律师费。孙主管当即表态按我的意见办：让王律师暂停代理，律师费不必收回，以后还用得着她。我很佩服他的敏锐和果断，趁热打铁提出与阳光公司签代理协议，他当场拍板。银行握有生杀予夺之权，彭和只能服从。 到处是雷区，到处是潜在的冲突。办这样一个变幻莫测的案子，一点不比指挥一场战役轻松。 三 赴京谈判 刚和彭和签完合同，胡杰就下了最后通牒：要么谈判，要么法院见。我的主意是谈，谈着拖，拖着谈。 我决定和彭和一起进京。彭和不想让我带助理，我没有同意：我和银行的合同总额虽是二百八十万，却按小时计费，多退少不补，必须有助理记录我的工作。彭和执意要从凯悦酒店搬到钓鱼台宾馆去住，说不能让人小瞧；又要我不承认律师身份，只说是他的法律顾问。我同意了，心里却觉得他未免太小心，胡杰一个走江湖的，还会怕一个律师？ 晚饭时，彭和的侄子彭大平也来了。他曾因袭警被关押，是我辩护才出来的。他说又有几个弟兄被平度公安抓了，非要我帮忙不可，我暂时答应下来。 当晚胡杰带着律师来了。他斜躺在沙发上，叼着中华烟，一见我就埋怨彭和带律师来。彭和说我是银行的律师，得罪不起。我表示自己只是来协调双方关系的：他们的关系理顺了，银行风险降低，按揭合同才能顺利执行。 胡杰说他的要求很简单，彭和还上一百五十万就行。我说，彭和账上的每一分钱都是银行的，他花钱银行当然要过问；胡杰连股权都没转让，就已拿走一千零五十万，几乎是空手套白狼，尾款等签了股权转让合同再付，合情合理。胡杰咆哮起来，说公司和法人都已变更，按合同半年前就该付清。我告诉他，这份合同在法律上无效，股权不转让，转让协议就是一张废纸，如果说有什么价值，就是可以作为抽逃资金的证据；他必须立即签署股权转让合同，否则可能涉嫌刑事犯罪。胡杰说他在北京从公安部到最高法院都有一帮哥们，接着打电话叫他的律师马上过来。彭和很紧张，怕我把事情搞砸。我安慰他，这是京城，一切都得按规矩来，何况我在这里读过七年书。 胡杰、韩菊带着律师进门，我和那位律师一照面都愣住了：他是我在法大读研究生时的同学陈律师。韩菊马上笑逐颜开，说都是熟人好办事，要请大家吃饭。陈律师说先谈案子。我抽出那份公司转让合同给他看，他看了一会儿，脸色发白。我说，你的老板就凭这张纸拿走了一千零五十万，而他的实际投资不到六百万，这个交易合法吗？胡杰急了，说他拿下那块地打点关系就花了二百多万。我只说了一句：“如果你说的是真的，那么问题更严重。” 陈律师听出了弦外之音，赶紧打圆场，说这笔交易不过是个不太规范的半拉子工程，当事人不是专业人士，出些纰漏很正常，可以完善，不能据此认定违法犯罪。我表示同意：这件事往好的方向发展，就是正当交易，大家都有钱赚；我们的意思一开始就是，他们痛快转让股权，我们付钱，决不食言。 胡杰却不肯松口。他说原合同没提股权转让，地还在我们手里，怕什么；签了字就有效，不给钱他就起诉，收回公司，那块地如今涨了好几倍，转手还能再赚一千万。我问他，公司既然已经转让，还攥着股权干什么？他说：“我就不转让股权，你能怎样？”我便不再谈，和陈律师握手道别，带着助理离开，身后传来胡杰的叫骂。彭和追出来埋怨我把人得罪了，我只回了一句：“让他走着瞧！” 四 找警察帮忙 第二天，陈律师来电话说，胡杰什么也听不进，执意起诉收回公司，还把他辞了。彭和害怕投资血本无归，我让他放心，胡杰的诉状到不了法庭。 我让彭和留在北京继续和胡杰周旋，自己先回青岛。我先找市经侦支队的同学张健给胡杰挂上号，再通过银行主管和行长找到市局分管经侦的副局长，以最快速度立了案。我本想带警察去北京抓人，副局长不同意，说既然是要阻止他到法院立案，在青岛等着他就是。我知道他们担心京城水深，怕出麻烦，就没有坚持。张健和我一起到市中级法院立案庭送达了一份协查通报，胡杰只要在中院露面，就会被立即控制。 一切安排妥当，我通知彭和撤回，临走时故意刺激胡杰，激他尽快来青岛起诉。 胡杰果然上当，一到青岛就落网了。警方对他采取监视居住，涉嫌罪名是抽逃注册资金和合同诈骗。这两个罪名能否成立，完全取决于我们的态度：如果我们配合他完善股权转让手续，抽逃资金就成了产权交易，合同诈骗也就子虚乌有。 胡杰被关在市公安局位于东海路的一座别墅的地下室里，起初绝食，三天后开始进食，七天后要求和我谈判。见面时他一扫往日的傲慢，表示认栽，任我提条件。我说这不是我的意思，而是法律的意思，我的主张没有变：完善股权转让手续，付给他尾款。胡杰垂头丧气地说，尾款不要也罢，先让他出去。 不付尾款不是我做事的原则。几天后，韩菊带着律师来到青岛，按法定程序转让了全部股权。阳光公司的合法性基石终于奠定。 目标完成，我通知彭和付款。但彭和耍赖，只付了四十九万，韩菊多次来电话大发雷霆，他仍拖着不付。 我已无暇顾及他们之间的烂账，因为彭和克扣工程款，许多工程队罢工，被拖欠工资的农民工到市政府上访，上千人堵住了市府周围的好几条街道。市长大发雷霆，建委和土地局组成的调查组开进工地，阳光公司的开发全面停止。 五 全面调停 银行非常愤怒，行长大骂彭和上不得台面，决定停发按揭贷款。我大吃一惊：银行已发放按揭款数千万，此时断供，项目必死无疑，银行的钱也一分都收不回来。我立即约见孙主管陈述利害，又打电话让彭和速回青岛解决问题。 彭和也知道自己闯了大祸，但他不去设法化解危机，反而私下和侯新生密谋，想学胡杰、韩菊的办法把项目转手，这样银行的风险就更大了。 我在海滨别墅约见彭和，告诉他转让项目既不可能，也很短视：一来银行不会答应，法院会立即查封冻结项目，侯新生也不会接这个烂摊子；二来这块地价格极低，建成后成本不过一千多元一平方米，房价一涨，卖三千、五千都有可能，现在转手就亏大了。彭和却诉苦说，政府不让干，银行不给钱，他没有办法。我说那就等着法院的传票吧。他见识过我对付胡杰的手段，对这句话非常害怕，马上软了下来，又是赔罪又是要请客。 我告诉他，要想复工，就立即给民工发工资，政府那边我去做工作。他叫苦说没钱，这要一百多万。我对他说：“商人有两种钱不能欠，一是政府的钱，二是打工者的血汗钱。”他小声嘟囔：“良心多少钱一斤？”我起身要走，他才连忙拦住，答应马上发工资。 我知道政府那边有银行牵着，只要市政府门口的农民工撤了，工作组就会撤走，政府也不愿看着项目成为烂尾工程。果然，彭和发了工钱，政府撤了工作组。可工程刚复工，又出了事：江苏盐城一家法院把传票送到了工地，还封了账户。 原来，一家江苏建筑企业在彭和的工地上承接工程，因拖欠材料款被外协单位起诉。这家企业是个空壳，在江苏没有财产，老板到庭后随口说在我们这里有二百万工程款，盐城法院便据此冻结了它在彭和公司账户上的所谓工程款。实际上，在工地干活的是一个包工头，只是借用了这家企业的资质和账户；而且因为农民工讨薪，他的工程款实际上已基本付清，彭和不可能替人还这笔冤枉债。问题在于，法院一封账户，按揭购房的老百姓人心惶惶，销售大受影响。更严重的是，彭和找来一帮江湖朋友，扣下了法院的人和车，非逼对方解封不可。 盐城法院报了警。平度法院和平度公安局没有市政府的指示，只能居中调解，双方僵持不下。法院的车被工地职工扣在银行门口，几名法官被平度的警察“解救”到市法院。警察说他们不懂民事法律，无从判断是非，于是彭和请我作为公司代理人与盐城法官交涉。 盐城来了四个人：两名法官、一名当事人和一名带着老式五四手枪的法警，看来是有备而来。我和彭和在宾馆与他们见面。姓于的庭长一见面就拍桌子，指责我们扣押法官的车，没有法律意识，警告说“天下法院是一家”，不马上放车后果很严重。彭和怪腔怪调地挖苦了一句，对方气得脸色煞白，气氛顿时紧张起来。 我先表示车很快就会送还，接着反问：我们不是本案当事人，冻结我们的账户合法吗？一位法官说他们有手续，要求我们协助执行。我说，连庭都没开，何来执行？对方解释这是保全措施的执行。我说，既然是保全，要我们协助，就应当先通知我们，而且只能冻结被申请人的账户，我们是被申请人吗？对方说这是司法惯例，以前都这样做。我说：“你们以前都这样做，只能证明你们身为法官却一贯违法，到底是谁的法律意识薄弱？” 于庭长招架不住，退一步说我们不服可以书面提出异议，不该扣车扣人。我指出，他们连书面法律手续都没给就封了账户，若不是发现及时，等他们回了盐城，我们的异议不知何时才能解决；况且工程的实际承包人并非他们的被告，被告只是被借用的名义，而我们公司早已不欠这家企业的钱，按初步估算，它完成的工程量还抵不上我们替它垫付的工人工资。法官们面面相觑，把目光转向当事人，当事人只能强辩说他只知道这里有工程款。 于庭长只好借坡下驴，同意当天解除查封，但要把我们列为共同被告，以查清真实的债权债务关系。我纠正说，只能列为无独立请求权的第三人，他同意了。 盐城法院解除了查封，我们也放了车。后来我们果然收到了追加第三人出庭的通知，我把政府付给农民工款项的支款明细表寄了过去，连庭都没出，案子便不了了之。 六 结局无言 一年后，房子全部建成，房价大涨，阳光花园的房子销售一空。原来一千二百元一平方米的房子卖到了三千多元，彭和净赚九千多万。 按代理合同，银行和彭和应支付我们二百八十万元律师费。但其中一百四十万被介绍此案的法官拿走，税也由我们承担，律师所实际到手只有二十五万。这笔钱主任分去一半，我只拿到十二万多一点，再扣除百分之四十的所里费用，所剩无几，其中还包括助理的费用和我的人情开销。几乎所有人都以为我发了大财，很多法官喝酒唱歌都打电话叫我去买单。每次去当冤大头，我总说：“我是大款，挣了二百八十万，我不买单谁买单？” 后来彭和见我实在寒酸，塞给我一个红包，说让我买件衬衫。走出他的办公楼，我发现红包里是一千元，便随手交给了团市委的微尘小姐。她正在做春蕾工程项目，把这笔钱分成两份：四百元给了城关一个残疾女孩，六百元给了店子镇一个失学女童。 我离开中国来到美国之后，家里还收到了这两个孩子寄来的感谢信。

content: 2026年11月20日 《刘晓波生死书》德译本的首次朗读 – 昨天在莱比锡沃尔夫-比尔曼九十歳的数千覌眾慶典音乐会上，譯员朗读了明年出版的《刘晓波生死书》德譯選段 ，引起极大轰動。另外，我表演了五分钟的洞箫和歌啸，自创曲目叫《沃尔夫和帕梅娜的河流舆时间》…… 最后，所有演出嘉宾都上台 …… 我给德国出版社主编汉斯写信道 : “从 著名記者 niels 的描述中，你们大约感受到了演出现场的热烈程度。最后，沃尔夫描述了他亲身经历过的、這本新书中的種種细节。他对我是那么推崇，我感动得不知道该说什么 。。。。。” 中文原文如下 – 我现在朗读流亡作家廖亦武将於2027发表的新书《Liu Xiaobo. Das Buch von Leben und Tod》選段。众所周知，刘晓波是2010年诺贝尔和平奖得主。他死于狱中，他的妻子刘霞被德国政府解救来德国。沃尔夫和帕梅拉在这一历史事件中，至关重要。希望未来的中国、德国、乃至全世界的人们，都能铭记这段历史。 – ……我开始写一生中最重要的信，收信人是德国总理安吉拉-默克尔。这封拉开正式营救序幕的长信，也全文收录在“刘晓波的最后时刻”中——当然，刘霞代表刘晓波、刘晖呈交“有关部门”的出国申请，原件和译文，都作为最重要的佐证，附在后面。 我在信中写道： ……2017年3月30日，刘晓波的妻子刘霞，坐火车从北京抵达辽宁省锦州监狱探监，向丈夫倾诉了自己的抑郁症和心脏病，母亲的绝症，以及弟弟刘晖受株连而被判刑十一年、至今仍被当作人质软禁在家的种种情况，此前毫不知情的刘晓波极为震惊、内疚和难过。他深爱自己的妻子，不忍见她继续受折磨，因此立即答应刘霞，携上妻弟刘晖，一道去德国……而此前，作为中国最有影响力的政治反对派领袖，也作为《零八宪章》的起草和发起人，坐牢四次的刘晓波一直表示，为推进中国未来的民主化，而绝不离开中国……我认为，通过默克尔夫人您和德国外交部低调而积极的交涉，刘晓波等人极有可能顺利降落柏林。原因是： 大约两年前，刘霞就有劝说丈夫一道来德国的强烈愿望，她在电话里向我多次诉说。我也将她的心愿多次向作家赫塔-穆勒夫妇、菲舍尔出版社主编彼得-西冷等好友转述，大家都非常担心。3月22号下午，我们再次相聚探讨方案，最后一致认为，虽然中国当局不太可能答应，但刘霞还是应该向负责监视她的秘密警察提出“向丈夫坦承实情，以劝说其出走”的要求……没想到，经过警方重重上报，上面出乎意料地批准了……这是一个明确信号： 如果中国当局不同意刘晓波出国，那么就会一如既往，不允许她透露实情，也不答应她的要求；也会掐断我和她在严密监控下的国际通话；也会掐断她和外界的联系，以防走漏风声…… – 当时我觉得，最具说服力的，是以上最末一段。稍后，在沃尔夫-比尔曼致默克尔的信中，也传递了他作为前东德过来人的跟进解读： – ……为什么绝不退让的刘晓波要放弃信念，从这“生死攸关”的游戏中抽身? 因为他面前摆着两种可能的选项：要么被监狱的万人坑埋没，要么尝试在欧洲过一种相对个人的生活。中国已有数百万殉难者。他们的案例让人愤怒也让人激动，可也把被害者压得瘫软绝望。现在看来，独裁政府更愿意把刘晓波这个人甩得远远的，最高决策层的利益考量也许是：如果把他放出去，他们的铁腕统治就少了一个受人拥戴的殉道者，他也就无法扰乱中国特色的暴政资本主义。这将是一个有利的双赢结局…… – 众所周知，安吉拉-默克尔是其时八十一岁的沃尔夫的密友，两人均来自前东德，据说少女时代的安吉拉就是沃尔夫的铁杆歌迷，几十年过去了，仍旧在繁忙政务之余，尽量照老习惯赶到沃尔夫夫妇的演唱会现场亮相助兴。 沃尔夫的父亲死于奥斯维辛集中营，母亲作为曾经抵抗纳粹的地下共产党员，却养出这么个坚决反共的儿子。1976年秋，沃尔夫逮住机会，从东柏林跑回西柏林，立即在科隆体育场举办挤满九千观众的个人演唱会，嘲讽和攻击共产主义阵营，其中有一首《长城内的中国》传诵一时：“在那里，人民像牲畜\被统治、被愚弄、被封口、被阉割\心甘情愿做牛马……\自由是一只死麻雀\在鸟笼里腐烂……\在中国！在中国！\在长城内的中国……” 演唱会尚未结束，实在受不了的东德最高当局就在柏林墙那边，通过高音喇叭宣告开除反党反革命分子沃尔夫-比尔曼的国籍，当即引发东西方冷战时期最为轰动的文化事件——岂料几十年后，沃尔夫又致信德国之声，将《长城内的中国》公开送给被十五次阻止出国的我。 由此，我也致信比尔曼夫妇： 親愛的的比爾曼和帕米娜： 我的患難之交，也是中國最大的政治犯劉曉波最近決定流亡德國。 我寫了一封信，向默克爾總理直接求助。我明白，只有你們能夠幫助我，以最快的速度，將它交到默克爾夫人手中。 這令我想起七年前，比爾曼為我寫的那幾段話和一首《長城下的中國》，我的朋友翻譯成中文讓我看……後來我就到德國了，在你們家壁爐旁听《長城下的中國》…… 親愛的比爾曼,時間過得可真快啊。 今天，輪到我向獄中的劉曉波伸出手了，但還得通過你。希望不久，你和帕米娜，也能見到劉曉波和劉霞，我們一起為他們舉辦音樂會。 你們的亦武 – 此信落款是2017年4月22日，经一再修改，24日通过正式和私下三个渠道寄出。接着是患得患失的等待。直至5月3日清晨9点多，户外天色晦暗，飘着濛濛细雨，通宵失眠的我，被突如其来的困意袭击，正要入梦，门铃却响了。 习惯早起的妻子璐在屋后院落伺候花草，听不见。门铃又响两次，我不得不起床穿衣，睡眼惺忪地开门守候。又过十来秒，一个身形硕大的白胡须老头从街面进到楼内，棕熊一般堵上门来。我用蹩脚的德语问了声好，他没回应，也没笑容，而是将捧在胸前的一个特大号硬壳纸信封递过来。我说等等，就转身去叫通晓德语的璐。不料，一回头，他就消失了。 这是沃尔夫-比尔曼派来的信使。后来帕梅娜说，这也是前东德时期的沃尔夫与反党反革命同伙秘密接头的方式。 我拆开不能复原的封口，原来是我写给默克尔总理的信件副本，沃尔夫用几行红字在右上角注明。令人心潮起伏的是，沃尔夫也给自己的铁杆粉丝安吉拉写了两千多字的长信，他说：“我来给他当这个信使。”他还说：“我们必须谨慎保密地做这件事。仅仅因几年前廖亦武在外交部长韦斯特维勒的帮助下经越南逃亡这事，已形成的外交沟壑仍无法被填平，当然也因为热衷炒作轰动消息的新闻界……” 就这样，默克尔执政时代有口皆碑的“静默外交”开始了。而在此前的4月28日，星期五，我也收到彼得-西冷如下的电子邮件: 亲爱的赫塔，亲爱的亦武，亲爱的哈瑞: 我已收到了外交部初步的回复，但没有任何关键性的内容。我估计，他们模棱两可的措辞，很可能是因为事情正在暗中进行。至少有一点很清楚，德国大使馆现在已经介入，从邮件中可以明显看出。我会尝试打电话了解更多情况。衷心希望事情进展顺利。 彼得 – 稍后，彼得-西冷再次从外交得到更为确切的消息，德国驻北京大使馆大使亲自致电刘霞，一一核实无误后，政府方面才指派专门的小组，主动联系中方，请求对口谈判。 资料照：中国著名异议人士、诺贝尔和平奖获得者刘晓波7月13日在中国沈阳病逝。 2017年7月13日，沃尔夫-比尔曼来信，告诉我营救失败，2010年诺贝尔和平奖得主刘晓波，和1935年诺贝尔和平奖得主卡尔-冯-奥西斯基一样，在几十名秘密警察的监控中死去。 – 刘晓波走了 亲爱的廖亦武， 刚刚传来消息：不是“我们做到了”，而是猪狗们得逞了，它们让你在中国的知心兄弟凋零逝去。今天，那个被折磨已久的人，也以他的方式成功了：刘晓波走了。帕梅拉（Pamela，比爾曼夫人）刚给我打了电话，告之这个消息。她眼下又在和我们的柏林女朋友交流，慎重保密一如既往。 可我们又面临一个新情况。不幸的是，当下我们只能竭力去营救万丈深渊边的寡妇了。你一定知道，我们在柏林的女朋友一直都在为刘晓波尽最大努力。啊，我亲爱的朋友，汉堡G20峰会的疯会、那些世界愤青们违背人性的愚蠢的暴戾狂欢、自由贸易的条约协议、熊猫外交、厄尔多安对恐怖主义的暗中援助和普京对叙利亚独裁者“英雄般的”搭救、被蚕食中的乌克兰、和中国超音速加集中营式资本主义做成的每一桩生意——抛开这一切，我们的努力永远是为了最最重要的目标：在弱肉强食的世界政治丛林里抢救一个作为个体的人。 帕梅拉建议我说：给亦武随信发去你当年写给我们的朋友尤尔根-福克斯（Jürgen Fuchs）那首歌吧。这很合适的！这位老兄也是作家，写诗歌和散文，在东德算是我一个年轻的知心兄弟。福克斯1976年在东柏林被捕，那正是我在11月被东德政府剥夺国籍的多事之秋。我们后来猜测，他在VEB人民监狱里被国安局的人秘密用伽玛射线施以辐射，悄无声息地种下了病根。1999年，年仅49岁的他死于血癌，成为此类放射受害者的典型案例。 我们把我们的朋友葬在了柏林的海德墓园（Heidefriedhof）。然后我和帕梅拉开车返回汉堡。因为时值五月，我们看到高速路两侧正在盛开的油菜花。特别在前东德区域，以前农业生产合作社广阔的土地上，只见咆哮怒放的巨大的黄。黄、黄、还是黄，直到天际。受此启发我作了这首歌，也许你能把它用中文、用同样的黄颜色调成诗，因为它的意蕴与刘晓波的命运相符。 不久你我一定会在柏林见面，那时我们会在柏林排练，和“中央四人乐团”（ZENTRALQUARTETT）的爵士乐手们练习我们的新歌，为了今秋在联邦议会选举前的“为民主巡演”（Demokratie-Tournee）。到时候我带上吉他，就能在你家给你、你妻子和女儿当面唱这只新歌了。 我用心灵拥抱你，我的朋友，希望能给你一些超越悲伤的安慰，因为逝去的是一位勇敢的斗士。正像诗人海涅在他《迷失的孩童》那首诗里写的，你的朋友刘晓波也是这样一位属于全人类的“在争取自由之战中孤陷重敌却坚守奋战”的人。 我下面这首歌的头两行也引自海涅的诗。 沃尔夫 2017年7月13日于汉堡-阿尔通纳 – 另：请把这些文字交给好手翻译，仅通晓两国文字是不够的。 – 给尤尔根-福克斯的輓歌 正是美得醉人的五月 无数枝芽鸟儿般纷飞 我的朋友却义无反顾 踏上那永无止境的旅程 他会在彼岸悠然等待 好吧，别辜负他的初心 随他而至，我们就在一起盼望 等我们美丽的女人 等我们心爱的女人 正当美得醉人的五月 一片片油菜花咆哮怒放 那夺目的黄色向我许诺 会给我朋友庇护与关怀 在那找不到出口的寒夜 他急需这一丁点太阳取暖 好让时间快些流逝 等我从此岸到来 等我从此岸到来 正当美得醉人的五月 一片片油菜花咆哮怒放 那夺目的黄色向我许诺 会给我朋友庇护与关怀 在那找不到出口的寒夜 他急需这一丁点太阳取暖 好让时间快些流逝 等我从此岸到来 等我从此岸到来   ————————————————————————————————- Lieber Yiwu und lieber Hans, einen lieben Gruß Euch beiden und Dir, lieber Yiwu, vielen lieben Dank für Deine Gedanken gestern am Abend für und mit Wolf Biermann, die Lesung in Erinnerung an Liu Xiaobo (und an Jürgen Fuchs) und Dein Lied. Es hat mich sehr bewegt, Dir und Chen Chen zuhören zu dürfen. Und ebenso, auch am Ende, zu sehen, wie groß die Verbundenheit zwischen Dir und Wolf Biermann ist. Danke für all das! Ich bin sehr froh, dass ich diesen besonderen Abend erleben durfte, mit so tollen, besonderen Menschen, darunter Du und Ihr. Bitte ganz liebe Grüße auch an Chen Chen. Und es war so schön zu sehen, dass Dein Freund Wolf eigentlich gar nicht aufhören wollte. So großartig! Meine Eltern, den Wolf Biermann in der DDR eine große Ermutigung war, sind so froh, dass wir ihm und Euch allen in Leipzig zuschauen und zuhören durften. Lieber Yiwu, ich danke Dir und freue mich sehr auf unser Wiedersehen im neuen Jahr, spätestens im Frühling. Und auf unser Gespräch über Liu Xiaobo. Wir bleiben in Verbindung. Heute alle guten Wünsche für Dich und Euch. Und in Verbundenheit. Euer Niels

title: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, bigger than others and nuclear-powered, nears completion
zh_title: 中国第四艘核动力航母即将完工
summary: 台湾新北市——分析人士称，中国的第四艘航空母舰是一艘迄今为止被称为 004 型的巨型舰艇，最早将于明年面世，其尺寸将比前几艘航母更大，并且配备核动力，在发生任何冲突时可以比平常更快地起飞飞机。这可能会增加日本和美国等已经对中国军队保持高度戒备的国家的压力。智库国防优先事项亚洲项目主任表示，目前正在北方港口城市大连建造的这艘航母部署后可容纳 75 至 90 架飞机。一个
content:
台湾新北市——分析人士称，中国的第四艘航空母舰是一艘迄今为止被称为 004 型的巨型舰艇，最早将于明年面世，其尺寸将比前几艘航母更大，并且配备核动力，在发生任何冲突时可以比平常更快地起飞飞机。这可能会增加日本和美国等已经对中国军队保持高度戒备的国家的压力。智库国防优先事项亚洲项目主任表示，目前正在北方港口城市大连建造的这艘航母部署后可容纳 75 至 90 架飞机。据智库战略与国际研究中心 (CSIS) 称，截至 10 月，该船的船体从未完工的船头到船尾长约 322 米，宽约 46 米。 CSIS 称 004 型“远大于中国海军任何其他级别的水面战斗舰”。新加坡南洋理工大学高级研究员科林·许 (Collin Koh) 表示，该航母的航拍照片显示“基本船体形式”已经建成，这预示着 2027 年发射的良好前景。他说，部署需要五到十年的时间。相关军事专家表示，自2025年政治争端以来，中国已在日本附近的海军存在“正常化”，考虑到其规模，包括海岸警卫队船只和海军军舰在内的庞大中国舰队可能已经瞄准了台湾的海上邻国日本。
Koh表示，这些规格将使004型航母比目前中国舰队中最大的一艘——中国的福建号航母“略大”。台北战略与兵棋推演研究委员会主席亚历山大·黄(Alexander Huang)表示，目前获得的有关004型航母的信息——可能会以中国现有的三艘航母等省份的名字重新命名——从电子设备、吨位和飞机运载能力方面将这艘航母归类为“超级航母”。 Koh说，机载核动力将为飞机提供比中国现有的电磁飞机发射系统更多的推进力。他表示，这将消除航母上对发电机的需求，同时允许更快的起飞（不影响有效载荷）和快速的战斗周转以加油。 “这似乎标志着某种战略目标，”高在谈到核能力时说道。 “它不仅仅会沿着你的海岸移动。它似乎标志着某种全球野心。”康奈尔大学专门研究军事历史和国防政策的教授大卫·西尔贝表示，核动力将使航母“基本上具有无限的续航能力”，并允许在全球部署，而无需常规动力航母所需的加油机支持。黄说，第四艘航母可能会部署到中国北方，因为其他三艘航母都在南方。
他说，在这种情况下，中国可以“利用这四种方式中的一种来始终在某个地方开展活动”。黄补充道，004型航母可能用于训练、维护以及作战。分析人士表示，中国的第四艘航母使其更接近与美国海军的竞争。西尔贝说，它的尺寸将与美国尼米兹级和福特级航母相当，这意味着它可以搭载多达 100 架飞机。 “这使得它比以前只能运载 50 架左右的航母具有更强的攻击力，”他说。美国海军拥有 11 艘航母，全部为核动力。高说，即使规模小于美国舰队，拥有核动力航母的中国海军也可以对美国构成挑战。美国海军在关岛保留基地

【原文 English Original】
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say. And it’s tipped to add pressure on countries, such as Japan and the United States, that already keep a high alert for the Chinese military. The carrier being built now in the northern port city Dalian could accommodate 75 to 90 planes once deployed, the Asia program director at the think tank Defence Priorities has said. As of October, the vessel’s hull measured about 322 meters in length from the unfinished bow to stern with a width of approximately 46 meters, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), also a think tank. CSIS called Type 004 “far larger than any other class of surface combatant” in China’s navy. Aerial photos of the carrier show the “basic hull form” already built, auguring well for a 2027 launch, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Deployment would take five to 10 years, he said. Related China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025 Given its scale, the massive Chinese flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say. The specs would make Type 004 “slightly larger” than China’s Fujian aircraft carrier, currently the biggest one in its fleet, Koh said. Information available today about the Type 004 – likely to be renamed after a Chinese province like the existing three – classify the vessel as a “supercarrier” in terms of electronics, tonnage and aircraft carrying capacity, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei. Nuclear power on board would offer the aircraft more propulsion than China’s existing electromagnetic aircraft launch system, Koh said. He said that would eliminate the need for power generators on board the carrier while allowing faster takeoffs – without payload compromises – and quick combat turnarounds for refueling. “It seems to signal a certain strategic objective,” Koh said of the nuclear capability. “It’s not just going to move along your coast. It seems to signal a certain global ambition.” Nuclear power will give the carrier “essentially unlimited endurance” and allow for global deployment without the kind of tanker support a conventionally powered carrier needs, said David Silbey, a Cornell University professor specializing in military history and defense policy. The fourth carrier may get posted to northern China because the other three are in the south, Huang said. In that scenario, he said, China could “use one of the four to always operate somewhere.” Type 004 may be used for training and maintenance as well as operations, Huang added. China’s fourth carrier gets it closer to rivaling the U.S. navy, analysts said. It will compare in size to the Nimitz and Ford class U.S. carriers, which means it can carry as many as 100 aircraft, Silbey said. “That gives it much more striking power than previous carriers, which could only carry around 50,” he said. The U.S. navy has 11 carriers, all nuclear powered. Even if smaller than the U.S. fleet, a Chinese navy with nuclear-powered carriers can mount a challenge to the United States, Koh said. The U.S. navy maintains bases in Guam, Hawaii and Japan plus treaty alliances with Japan and the Philippines. The U.S. and China have long seen each other as rival superpowers. Experts have said China sent an especially large number of its naval deployments near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political rift that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The Philippines is embroiled in a maritime sovereignty dispute with China. China plans to build more carriers over the next decade for a “blue water capability that they’ve never really had before,” Silbey said. “In the Pacific, it means that they can go after American assets that are out of range of their other assets.”

互动：跟踪 COP31 气候峰会上的谈判文本 互动：在 COP31 气候变化峰会上谁想要什么 由于严重分歧阻碍了就主席主导的协议达成一致，《联合国气候变化框架公约》主席西蒙·斯蒂尔表示“深感失望”，他谈到了联合国气候进程的“改进、现代化和改革的空间”。闭幕全体会议。其中包括为全球“公正转型”建立新“机制”的相当有限的或程序性的成果，以及对遭受气候灾难的国家的支持。不过，谈判之外还取得了一些进展，越来越多的国家联盟倡导“摆脱”化石燃料的“路线图”。随着主席国推动“电气化”成为关键主题，约 80 个国家还签署了到 2035 年确保 35% 的最终能源消耗来自电力的全球目标。在此，Carbon Brief 深入分析了安塔利亚会议在 COP31 谈判内外的所有关键成果。

Print article Share Article Contents Expand menu Close Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance . The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations. Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation. COP31 coverage COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31 Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’? Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process. Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary. These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “ mechanism ” for global “ just transitions ”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters. There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “ roadmaps ” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. With the presidency promoting “ electrification ” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations. (See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30 , COP29 , COP28 , COP27 , COP26 , COP25 , COP24 , COP23 , COP22 , COP21 and COP20 .) Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Guidance on NDCs Rio synergies Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges. Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted. Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer. Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years . In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”. COP31 president and Turkish minister Murat Kurum and COP31 “president of negotiations” and Australian minister Chris Bowen. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion. Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production. Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31. The first letter , written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October. The second letter , authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”. The third letter , published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “ action agenda ” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further. This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification .) The final letter , published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”. It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding: “At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.” The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . A crowded roadbridge near the COP31 entrance in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”. He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues. On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision .) At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down. On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations. Countries take part in a “divan” at COP31. Credit: UNFCCC / Flickr Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening. In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday. Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”. However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision .) On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge. Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.  In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.  They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.  An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”. As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. width: 64px; align-self: start; } } Membership Support award-winning climate journalism Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.  Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious –  closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .)  While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised… Read more on CB Connect → This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations. The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target , as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels .) A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs. This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation .) It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”. Paragraph 36 of the second draft cover text. Source: UNFCCC . Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “ quid pro quo ” for the quantified electrification target. The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”. Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro. A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit. This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”. Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups. They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.) The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted. However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports. On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.” But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful. The UK told the closing plenary: “What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.” Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures. Saudi Arabia, for the Arab group, said that they had continued to “engage constructively” on the cover decision, “despite all of the issues that were taken off the table”, including on finance and historical emissions . It also said: “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5C within reach and, yet, calling CCUS technologies greenwashing.” Russia explained its steadfast opposition to “any wording on fossil fuels” – despite the wording agreed by consensus at COP28. It criticised “slogans” around the use of fossil fuels, arguing that even in 1.5C pathways, there was an ongoing role for oil and gas. While the failure to adopt a cover decision has been widely compared to the collapsed Copenhagen climate talks in 2015, experts told Carbon Brief this comparison was flawed. Nevertheless, they said it could end the recent trend of COPs attempting to secure a cover decision, as well as sparking renewed reflections on how to reform the process. Paul Watkinson , the French chief negotiator at Paris COP21, told Carbon Brief: “This time it is the political bet of the presidency on a cover decision that has not worked…I think this needs a deeper reflection on what we are trying to achieve – there are limits to political signals in a decision – and we ought to think [about] what we can achieve through the COP and how to make it work better.” The failure of the Antalya pact meant that initiatives on oceans, methane, mountains – and on COP reform itself – were all lost from the formal outcome of the summit. While some may be revisited at future COPs, not all have a clear place on the agenda. COP reform As COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed “Antalya pact”, much of the immediate response focused on perceived shortcomings in the UN climate process. In his closing remarks , UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell said there were “lessons that must be learned” for the consensus-driven process: “Clearly, there is also scope to improve, modernise and reform. But not only because of what happened here. But also because we must evolve in this era of implementation.” In fact, one of the COP31 presidency’s stated priorities had been reforming COPs – or what they described as “strengthen[ing] UNFCCC processes”.  COP reform was discussed during the summit, including at a press conference where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro told journalists: “The COP has become an exercise in futility…192 countries will not agree on every single comma and every single period…especially those countries that produce carbon-based fuels.” In practice, such bombastic statements were far removed from the on-going discussions and country submissions on COP reform , which had already begun in Brazil last year.  These discussions were integrated into the formal negotiations under the heading of “ arrangements for intergovernmental meetings ” (AIM).  At the Bonn climate talks in June, Australia, along with Turkey, offered to conduct informal consultations on increasing UNFCCC “efficiency” at COP31.  The African group asked for legal clarity and cautioned that “efficiency should not be equated with reducing budgets or removing agenda items” necessary to tackle climate change, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  Early in the talks, the COP31 presidency published a concept note calling for “forward-looking and exploratory” discussions on what a “strong and effective UNFCCC process” could look like. It also initiated “presidency consultations” on the matter, despite the lack of a clear mandate for doing so. In the presidency consultations, responses included multi-year planning, retiring old agenda items and “avoiding unnecessary cover decisions”.  Several countries – including Russia, the African group, AILAC and the LMDCs – questioned the need for separate discussions and whether these were solely for the cover decision, given they were already underway in the AIM negotiations.  Russia said it “did not consent to elevating this discussion to high political level” and that it was unclear “why such a significant amount of negotiating time [was] being devoted” to these roundtables without a clear objective.  Drafts of the presidency’s failed cover decision included “high-level consultations” under COP presidencies on “strengthening the UNFCCC process”. During the final plenary, Peru, for AILAC, called for a “clear rule on votes” and an independent review of the COP process’s efficiency. Peru’s environment director Andrés Martín Garrido Sánchez said: “To negotiate in good faith is not a courtesy; it’s an obligation. It means not using delays as a strategy. It means negotiating text in the room in the view of everyone, with every party being heard before a decision is gavelled. It means not taking issues hostage…We are not proposing matters against the consensus. This way of negotiating is not leading us to where the world needs us to be.”  With the Antalya pact rejected, these discussions will still continue under AIM in Bonn in 2027. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Adaptation While efforts to specify that tripling adaptation finance meant $120bn by 2035 failed to make it into any final texts, COP31 did see a breakthrough on channelling carbon-market revenues into the UN adaptation fund . Disagreements over finance dominated negotiations within the “ global goal on adaptation ” (GGA).  This followed a “call for efforts” to triple adaptation finance by 2035, which was agreed last year at COP30. That target was originally proposed by the LDCs as a “tripling of grant-based adaptation finance by 2030 to at least $120bn”.  Last year’s final agreement was considerably weaker and lacked key details – including the baseline for tripling and what kinds of funding would be counted towards it. Ahead of the start of COP31, the African group requested that the tripling goal be added to the agenda, providing a potential space to discuss these outstanding issues. African group request for agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. Source: UNFCCC . This request was rejected . As a result, the question of where the goal should be discussed quickly arose as a fault line. It was debated within the GGA, the climate finance “work programme”, as well as the proposed “cover decision”.  As negotiations got underway, the G77 and China coalition of developing countries argued that adaptation finance should be discussed in the GGA rooms.  The EU, UK, environmental integrity group (EIG), Norway and Canada all wanted adaptation finance discussed under the climate finance work programme. This would place the tripling goal within the broader $300bn target for 2035 – meaning adaptation finance could come from a wide variety of sources, not just developed-country grants. Over the first week of negotiations, two GGA draft texts were released, both of which included specific references to tripling adaptation finance to $120bn per year by 2035.  This would use a baseline of 2025, when the previous target to double adaptation finance to $40bn per year came to an end.  Draft GGA text on 13 November. Source: UNFCCC . Over the second week of COP31, parties continued to disagree over the home and baseline for the tripling target.  The first draft text on the cover decision – reflecting ideas put forward by parties – included relatively ambitious language that tripling finance for adaptation “should reach at least $120bn”. However, the “$120bn” was absent from the next draft and an accompanying GGA text . NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported that France – as co-chair of the ministerial climate-finance negotiations – had proposed a 2019 baseline, which would reduce the tripling target to just $60bn a year by 2035.  For context, the latest UNEP report on adaptation suggests that developing countries will need a total of $305bn every year by 2035 to meet their adaptation needs. Ultimately, neither the GGA, the climate finance work programme nor the failed cover decision specifically contained a baseline or target figure for tripling adaptation finance. Bethan Laughlin , senior policy specialist at ZSL (Zoological Society of London), told Carbon Brief that the failure to agree a baseline does a “colossal amount of damage, because it is a continued betrayal of promises for finance of all types”.  Beyond finance, parties worked to establish an expert taskforce that could refine the set of 59 “indicators” for the global goal on adaptation, which had been agreed at COP30, as part of the two-year “Belém-Addis vision”. These are the metrics that countries will use to assess their progress in adapting to climate change. Speaking to Carbon Brief, Emilie Beauchamp , senior adaptation expert at International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ), highlighted that the indicators had been pushed through in Brazil without full engagement from parties. She added:   “It ties into the bigger picture, which is that [the] Brazilian presidency’s cover decision didn’t leave any space for countries not to adopt these 59 indicators. These are complex and incomplete, which means most countries aren’t happy with them.” Parties agreed on the need for a “two-tier” approach to resolving this, with a taskforce undertaking technical work on the indicators and then a policy alignment process for testing them. However, the composition of the taskforce quickly became a sticking point, just as it had in Bonn earlier in the year, according to ENB .  The 19 November draft GGA text still contained three options on the taskforce’s composition, including a mix of experts nominated either by regions, the chairs of the UNFCCC subsidiary bodies or by UN organisations and other non-party stakeholders.  Parties also disagreed on references in the GGA text to the Paris Agreement and “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” ( CBDR-RC ), plus on recognition of the importance of the 1.5C goal in limiting the need for adaptation.  While the final decision agreed at COP31 does not mention overshoot or 1.5C, it does provide clarity on the taskforce. It “agrees” that six experts will be nominated per UN regional group, in addition to three experts nominated by the LDCs and three by small island developing states.  With so much time and focus given to the finance question, smaller technical aspects of the GGA negotiations struggled to find consensus across the two weeks of COP31.  Laughlin said:  “I think we are seeing these big-number finance issues as absolutely fundamental, but we’re also seeing the technical elements of the process, where the real work of implementation is done, be significantly challenged and, in my view, denigrated into obsolescence.” Observers told Carbon Brief that there had not been sufficient time given to the GGA, as well as items such as national adaptation plans (NAPs). One said that more than double the negotiating time had been devoted to the cover decision than to mandated items, such as the GGA, MWP and JTWP, over the first week.  Beauchamp told Carbon Brief she hoped that COP32 president Ethiopia would “break this pattern”.  Beyond the GGA, other adaptation items also proved challenging at COP31.  G77 and China huddle during informal consultations on national adaptation plans. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis. The adaptation fund is the oldest dedicated UN climate fund and was set up as part under the Kyoto Protocol. Now, it is in the process of transitioning to exclusively serve the 2015 Paris Agreement. This will allow it to access 5% of the revenues generated by the agreement’s Article 6.4 carbon market. This process has previously been delayed by disagreements over the makeup of the fund’s board.  The expectation has been that under the Paris Agreement, the board would have set quotas for “developed” and “developing” nations – the terms used in the treaty – instead of “Annex I” and “non-Annex I” nations, as it has done in the past. Some parties see this distinction as important, because the UNFCCC annexes clearly separate a small group of predominantly European and industrialised states from other nations, whereas the “developed-developing” division is less clearly defined. Joe Thwaites , international climate finance director at Natural Resources Defense Council , told Carbon Brief that parties “can’t access” the Article 6.4 “share of proceeds” until this is resolved. A draft text released on 18 November continued to include references to both “developed countries” and parties “included in Annex I to the convention” within square brackets.  Ultimately, the final decision confirmed that there will be regional quotas instead of “developed” and “developing”, but it also confirmed that developing countries will continue to have a majority of seats on the board. Thwaites described the resolution of the adaptation fund negotiations as “one bright spot” from the climate summit, noting: “The decisions at COP31 enable the fund to receive a share of carbon-trading proceeds under the Paris Agreement crediting mechanism, which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes.”  Negotiations on NAPs , adaptation communications and adaptation committee discussions all ended with procedural conclusions, meaning no substantive agreement was reached.  One adaptation area with more progress was “matters relating to the LDCs”, an agenda item where parties discuss support and adaptation planning for the 44 LDCs .   Despite “difficult negotiations”, on the second Wednesday of COP31, parties agreed to a decision that establishes a “LDCs national adaptation plan implementation platform” under the LDCs expert group.  ENB quoted a delegate saying: “This decision may not make the headlines, but it means a lot for the more than one billion most vulnerable people who benefit from the work under this agenda item.” Finance As COP31 ended in disputes and finger-pointing, a major complaint by many parties was the failure to agree progress on climate finance. In their closing speeches, several developing-country figures expressed “profound concern”, accusing developed countries of “refusing to engage” on this “essential” issue.  Finance talks ended with little – beyond decisions to hold more meetings. There was no progress on “tripling adaptation finance”, despite efforts to flesh out this goal. (See: Adaptation .)  Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts by developed countries and, as revealed by Carbon Brief, a corresponding 70% drop in the amount of public climate funding being pledged. COP31 co-president Australia drew heavy criticism from NGOs for failing to commit new funds, along with other major donors, such as Germany, France and Japan.  Meanwhile, pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years, with few new commitments in Antalya.  Protesters at COP31 calling for climate finance. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Two years ago, nations agreed on a “ new collective quantified goal ” (NCQG), which involves developed countries “taking the lead” in raising $300bn in climate finance a year by 2035. A variety of sources are expected to feed into this goal, including multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and private finance “mobilised” by public investments.  In recent years, roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries. The provision of funds by these nations now looks less certain , amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending. Developing countries, therefore, came to COP31 looking for assurances. Finance was discussed across most rooms in Antalya, but negotiations around a climate finance “ work programme ” – set up at COP30 last year – were the main venue for this push. Developing countries had wanted to create this space to discuss finance “provision” under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which says developed countries “shall provide” finance. This is taken to mean public funding – such as aid spending – from developed countries. (The NCQG, on the other hand, is a “mobilisation” goal, meaning it covers various funding sources, including private finance “mobilised” by public investments.) This came amid concerns that developed countries were trying to transfer responsibility onto others. Abdulkani Barrow , Somalia’s lead negotiator, told Carbon Brief: “Africa does not want developed countries’ historical financial responsibilities to become diluted by a general expectation that private investors, developing countries and other financial actors should provide the money.” However, due to pressure from developed countries, the work programme was set up with a broader remit, including Article 9.1 “in the context of Article 9…as a whole”.  Following initial talks in June, the programme was only added to the COP31 agenda due to a continued push by developing countries. The EU remained “deeply concerned” about its inclusion.   Coming into COP31, developing countries continued to insist that the work programme should focus exclusively on Article 9.1.  Some developing-country groups, notably the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and the Arab group , said it should consider ways to secure more from developed countries, including “burden-sharing arrangements”. They also argued for an extensive new set of talks and other activities. Extract from “work programme on climate finance” text from 15 November, showing an option for “burden-sharing arrangements”. Source: UNFCCC . Such ideas were unacceptable for developed countries, who generally wanted a far more limited set of actions that were “non-prescriptive” and “non-punitive”.  They argued that the talks should be based on the existing $300bn mobilisation goal, stressing that they were already contributing tens of billions a year. Prior to COP31, Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”. (This statement – and choice of words – sparked outrage among civil society and was even quoted by India’s Amandeep Garg in the closing plenary.) Speaking at the climate summit, Hoekstra told Carbon Brief: “We made a deal with the whole world community on financing…We don’t think there is any merit in opening it.” (The work programme was established “without prejudging the process for the implementation of the NCQG”.) There were a few finance-related issues that the EU and their allies were happy to discuss, including “broadening the contributor base” to include wealthier developing countries. Developed-country groups also said they wanted the discussions about “ tripling adaptation finance ” to take place within the work programme, as part of the NCQG. This would mean adaptation finance coming from both their public spending and other sources . In particular, the EU, the UK and others said they wanted to discuss “access” – helping small islands and other low-capacity nations to better get hold of the finance that already exists. Ilana Seid , chair of AOSIS, told Carbon Brief that this focus on access presented small-island states with “an interesting dilemma”, because they also needed more finance, noting: “The whole machinery needs to move.” The developed countries’ stated focus on access amounted to little, with no mention in the final finance decision . The Australian presidency was set to launch an “ access declaration ” for small islands and LDCs at COP31 – but the event was cancelled, partly due to lack of signatories. After drafts circulated , the first official work programme text landed at the start of the second week. It contained two lengthy, opposing sets of “options”, which broadly reflected the competing priorities of the developed and developing-country blocs. This was reflected in the next iteration , which had a set of brackets around the entire document.  NGOs said the EU was acting as a “ villain ”. Sehr Raheja , deputy programme manager at the Centre for Science and Environment , told Carbon Brief: “If they’re derailing the negotiations on this work programme, then that commitment to the NCQG – in my mind – is questionable.” Co-chairs of the finance negotiations attempted to combine the work-programme discussions with another set of talks on Article 2.1c of the Paris Agreement – which relates to “making finance flows consistent” with climate goals.  Developing countries objected to this effort. They wanted to keep discussions focused on the responsibilities of developed countries, rather than broadening them to all “finance flows”. As COP31 drew to a close, it became clear that a stripped-back outcome was likely for both the work programme and Article 2.1c negotiations, with nothing substantial on finance provision, tripling adaptation finance or any other stated party priorities. This was reflected in the final decisions , which contained largely procedural outcomes. Notably, parties did agree to continue discussing finance under the work programme until 2028, rather than ending next year as some developed countries preferred . Less high-profile finance texts, such as the Standing Committee on Finance , also finished with largely procedural outcomes.  Just transition work programme Discussions on how to create a new “ just transition mechanism ” (JTM) proved one of the most controversial aspects of COP31 and were, ultimately, deferred to COP32.  At COP30 last year, negotiations under the broader “just transition work programme” (JTWP) had agreed to launch the mechanism, a decision seen as a key “ legacy ” of the summit. At COP31, parties were expected to agree on the form and function of the mechanism, to allow it to start working.  Following work in Bonn in June and a workshop in Sydney in the autumn, parties began negotiations in Antalya productively, with general consensus emerging on a two-tier structure for the mechanism. This would include a political and governance body, as well as a technical operational arm, according to Earth Negotiation Bulletin (ENB). Similarly, despite some divergences on the duration and scope of the work programme, there was broad support for the continuation of the JTWP beyond 2026. This initial work suggested that the JTM – referred to as the Belem-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) by civil society – would have a similar format to that previously suggested by NGOs and academics.  However, a draft text prepared at the end of the first week of negotiations was met with criticism from civil society, due to its lack of substantive detail on the mechanism.  They told Carbon Brief in statements that it was “hollow”, “watered-down” and an “insult to the principles parties agreed in Brazil”, adding that the “exciting potential for COP31 to deliver a real just transition mechanism is hanging by a thread”.  Speaking to Carbon Brief, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins , a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want , said there had been a “steep decline” in negotiations.  He added that developed parties, such as the EU, Norway and the UK, were pushing for the mechanism to run dialogues, produce reports and connect people. He said that while this was “fine”, it is largely already happening in the JTWP and would have little impact on implementation.  Sealey-Huggins continued: “G77 and China have been really strong on pushing back on that in various different ways. [They are] united in the call for some kind of institutional arrangement that will have longevity, that will have power to implement work and that will do the work of scaling up means of implementation [and] support.”  Over the second week, the key areas of focus became who would set up and run the mechanism, the involvement of non-party stakeholders and how it would be financed. The G77 and China, African group and LDCs shared proposals on how the mechanism could deliver implementation. The EU and EIG highlighted the role of non-party stakeholders. Anabella Rosemberg , senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group CAN International , told Carbon Brief that the arrival of ministers in the second week put a “cold wind in our room”. She said that what should have been a “relatively easy win” for COP31 was disrupted by disagreements in other areas, including finance and mitigation. Throughout the second week, there was also criticism of the Turkish presidency’s involvement in the JTWP. On 17 November, it was given a “dishonourable mention” in CAN’s “ fossil of the day ” award. This followed COP31 president Murat Kurum saying during a ministerial roundtable:  “Rather than creating new structures, it would be more favourable to establish a system that better connects existing resources.” Parties and civil society were quick to criticise the statement, which they viewed as breaching presidential neutrality.  As the summit progressed, negotiations became further mired in disagreement. Rosenberg told Carbon Brief they were hampered by the focus on the cover decision, which “basically captured the oxygen of the negotiations”.  On 19 November, a new JTWP draft text was published. However, the entire body of it was contained within square brackets. Key issues, such as the institutional arrangements for the new mechanism, were still only mentioned as “options”.  A call from the G77 and China for the mechanism to be a “constituted body”, meaning a specialised subsidiary that would house work on the mechanism would be established under the UNFCCC, was not included, observers told Carbon Brief.   Civil society – who originally proposed the mechanism – became increasingly vocal as COP31 moved into its final scheduled day. At a packed press conference attended by Carbon Brief, speakers said it had been “possibly the worst COP in history” and that they “unequivocally reject” the outcomes as they stood.
