She added:  “Damage control is not a victory at this point. This is a failure of ambition and leadership, particularly from the so-called ‘developed countries’, who obstruct the provision of support, and of the COP31 presidency, who sidelined the united calls from 135 countries – almost 80% of the global population.” Beyond the mechanism, parties discussed a review of the JTWP and the key messages that emerged from the fifth and sixth just-transition “dialogues” held in 2026. Over the two weeks of negotiations, parties disagreed on language around agriculture and other topics, as well as the inclusion of references to transitioning away from fossil fuels and trade – neither of which made it into the final decision.  At COP30 last year, references to minerals had been included in earlier drafts on the JTWP – the first time they had appeared in a text within the UNFCCC process. However, this did not make it into the final decision in Belém.  At COP31, “critical minerals” were referenced in a COP decision for the first time.  In a statement, Angela Asuncion , Asia-Pacific coordinator and transition-minerals focal point at the Resource Justice Network , welcomed the inclusion as a “notable step”, but added that “the decision by parties to eliminate human rights due diligence across critical mineral supply chains is unacceptable”. She added:  “Stripping away these fundamental safeguards is a profound failure of leadership. By failing to operationalise the BAM and removing human-rights safeguards in critical-mineral operations, governments have once again abandoned frontline communities.” Loss and damage Negotiations on “ loss and damage ” resulted in few substantial outcomes at COP31 and only limited recognition of the gap in funding to aid victims of climate disasters. On top of finance to support emissions cuts and climate adaptation, developed countries are expected to take the lead on this issue. Loss-and-damage funding has been particularly in the spotlight since the devastating Himalayan floods over the summer. The Nepali government subsequently requested $20m from the UN fund for loss and damage , which was established with much fanfare at COP27 in 2022. So far, predominantly developed nations have pledged just $342m to the fund, a fraction of the $2.8bn in funding requests that developing countries have submitted. The fund’s board does not plan to start distributing finance until December, despite pressure to begin fast-tracking applications in response to urgent needs. Speaking at a COP31 side event , Nepali environment minister Gita Chaudhary said “disasters do not wait for the paperwork and neither can survivors”. She added: “The gap between the scale of loss and damage and the resources available in the fund is enormous and growing, so Nepal, therefore, strongly urges developed country parties to honour their commitments.” Gita Chaudhary, environment minister of Nepal, at COP31. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Unlike previous years , very little new loss-and-damage funding was announced at COP31 – limited to €15m ($16.5m) from Spain , plus Italy and the EU formalising previous pledges. The fund’s first replenishment process is due to start in 2027. In negotiations, parties were tasked with discussing a report on the loss and damage fund and deciding what guidance – if any – they wanted to provide for its operation.  Explaining why such guidance might be necessary, Liane Schalatek , an associate director and climate-finance expert at Heinrich Böll Stiftung , told Carbon Brief: “From developing countries, there have been concerns about things that are happening in the board meetings…There is no sense of urgency from developed countries to figure out how and when we do resource mobilisation.” An initial text presented two options. The first – favoured by the African group, LDCs and AOSIS – laid out six pages of guidance for the fund, “noting with concern” the gap between funding available and requests made. The alternative, supported by the EU and Japan, simply stated “no guidance”. They cited concerns about “ micromanaging ” the fund’s board. The final text “noted” the loss-and-damage finance shortfall, but contained relatively weak language about the need to scale up funding. One exception was a line “urg[ing] the conversion of pledges as soon as possible”, referring to promised funds that have not yet been paid out. Meanwhile, there were technical discussions at COP31 involving the joint annual report of the executive committee of the Warsaw International Mechanism (WIM) and the Santiago Network , plus the governance of the WIM. These two bodies are involved in research and helping developing countries access technical assistance to deal with loss and damage. One key dispute in these negotiations concerned WIM governance, which has gone unresolved for several years , but has not prevented the body from undertaking its work.  In the end, parties decided to simply defer the issue again, with a footnote in the final decision stating that this does not “prejudge outcomes” on WIM governance. Gender There was limited progress on negotiations on gender in Antalya, as a small number of parties once again pushed back on language on inclusion.   At COP30 last year, parties agreed on the Belém gender action plan (GAP), which set out specific actions for ensuring gender-responsive climate action and indicators for measuring parties’ progress on gender-related issues. This year’s summit was expected to be a “simple procedural negotiation”, with parties meant to discuss several reports that were deliverables under the GAP, said Bridget Burns , executive director of the Women’s Environment and Development Organization (WEDO).  However, she told Carbon Brief: “Our experience has shown us that even the most insignificant procedural negotiations can also get quite derailed and that’s somewhat what happened here.” During the first consultations, on 10 November, the co-facilitators sought parties’ views on three reports prepared by the secretariat, according to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB).  ENB said that several negotiating groups used their time to highlight the need for finance, capacity-building and technology transfer in order to effectively implement the GAP. The first draft of the text, released late that day, “welcome[d]” the three reports and the work conducted under the GAP during its first year. It also “t[ook] note” of a report on addressing reported cases of harassment at the UNFCCC, but did not significantly mention the need for additional means of implementation. On the second day of consultations, the G77 and China reportedly asked for stronger language on finance, which was reflected in brackets in the text’s second draft , as shown below. A paragraph recognising the need for support for developing countries to implement gender action. Source: UNFCCC . Later in the first week, several parties objected to the use of inclusive language. They also disagreed over whether they should “welcome” or “take note” of the secretariat’s reports. (The latter is considered to be weaker language .) As at last year’s summit, Argentina, Paraguay, Russia and the Holy See – the government of the Vatican – raised objections over the use of previously agreed, gender-inclusive language in the draft.  Burns told Carbon Brief that it was “continually jarring” to see the Holy See “huddling with Russia in almost every negotiation stream”. She added: “The Holy See has been specifically vocal in these negotiations…and, in my opinion, [are] disastrously using the moral capital that they have to drive this process into procedural negotiations that are meaningless to actually changing what has been [previously] adopted in this process.” The final text , published on 14 November, reflected the lack of consensus, simply saying that the SBI had “considered” the reports and “acknowledged” the work being done to implement the GAP. Noemi Grütter , head of advocacy and partnerships at the Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action , told Carbon Brief that, despite the lack of progress on the agenda item, important work on implementation is still happening on the ground. She added: “There is also the reality that we need to build power outside of UNFCCC, because it’s not fast enough. There are countries that are willing [to do that], and I think we need to work with them.” According to the Guardian , Argentina and Paraguay both intervened over the definition of gender in the plenary during the adoption of the standing finance committee decision in the early hours of Sunday morning. Article 6 Negotiations at COP31 on carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement reopened many familiar arguments over how tightly such activities should be regulated. Beatriz Granziera , senior policy adviser at The Nature Conservancy (TNC), told Carbon Brief: “Discussions repeatedly came back to familiar trade-offs: practicality versus conservativeness; flexibility versus oversight; and how to scale much-needed participation and investment while maintaining environmental integrity.” Agreement was, ultimately, reached on both bilateral trading under Article 6.2 and the international carbon market under Article 6.4. Carbon trading between countries under Article 6.2 is only subject to light-touch rules, such as reporting on the use of the process and a “technical expert review” of national reports. Across 16 national reports checked so far, these reviews found 543 “inconsistencies”, 115 of which were “significant”. None of the reports were found to be without issue. An initial draft text at Antalya “note[d these issues] with concern”, adding that “many…are significant” and relate to “environmental integrity” – in other words, whether or not emissions are actually being cut. It asked parties to address issues “at the earliest opportunity”. However, this entire paragraph disappeared in the final, agreed text . Instead, the decision “takes note” of the information in the technical reports, without asking for any response. Given its confidentiality provisions, campaign groups have long described Article 6.2 as a “ wild west ” for carbon trading and the COP31 outcome does nothing to tighten the rules. Separately, parties were unable to reach agreement at COP31 on how to fund the processes needed to run Article 6.2. Instead, they agreed to continue discussions next year, requesting a technical paper on how “fees or other funding arrangements” would work. On Article 6.4, negotiations began against a backdrop of calls for a “ course correction ” on the way the international carbon market is operated. This came in an open letter from the Project Developer Forum and the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), saying market rules were too “conservative”. Andrea Bonzanni , senior director at IETA, told Carbon Brief that the “current version of [the market] is failing to attract investment in carbon projects”. The requests in the open letter appeared in early draft text, after being taken up by the like-minded developing countries and others. A 14 November draft “request[ed]” the supervisory body to “assess the cumulative impact” that its rules and standards have on the “feasibility” and “cost” of carbon-credit schemes. It said this was to avoid “excessive compounding of conservative adjustments”, in what amounted to asking that the rules for the Article 6.4 market not be too stringent. Draft text of 14 November on Article 6.4. Source: UNFCCC . Isa Mulder , at Carbon Market Watch , told Carbon Brief that this looked like market proponents “chipping away at the standards that have been set out”. She added: “The goal [of Article 6] was to enable higher ambition, not to enable [carbon-trading] activities.” However, after pushback from the EU and others, the final text adopted at COP31 no longer asks for a formal assessment of the “cumulative impact” of the rules. Instead, it asks that the supervisory body “take into account” the way different standards “operate together” when making or revising provisions. Towards the end of the summit, 45 scientists signed an open letter saying that the Article 6 rules “must be consistent with the science”. With those rules set for a review starting in 2028, Granziera told Carbon Brief: “Ultimately, the debate [at COP31] reflected different views on what is needed for Article 6 to deliver more effectively as a tool for achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement, which will likely come back to light in 2028.” Agriculture and food security For the second year in a row, negotiations on the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture (SJWA) collapsed without parties reaching an agreement.  SJWA is where formal negotiations around climate change and agriculture take place under the UNFCCC.  Part of SJWA’s mandate is to synthesise information about work being done in the agricultural space – under both the UNFCCC and other international bodies – in an annual report.  SJWA also held two workshops – one on holistic approaches to agriculture and one on “means of implementation”, usually taken to mean finance – where countries and other partners could share their experiences, as captured in summary reports. At this COP, parties were meant to discuss the conclusions of these reports and, time permitting, decide on the future of the agricultural workstream under the UNFCCC. (The four-year mandate of SJWA was set to end at COP31.) Many observers were hopeful of agreeing a text that recognised agroecology as beneficial for humans, climate and biodiversity.  However, in the first negotiating session, on 10 November, the Arab group expressed its view that fertilisers are vital for food security and fertiliser exports are being impacted by the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Therefore, it said, the agriculture talks needed to discuss CBAM and other trade measures. Teresa Anderson , global climate-justice lead at ActionAid , called this a “total curveball” in the negotiations. She told Carbon Brief: “Everybody’s faces just dropped…Suddenly we knew that the chances of agroecology having a chance had been pretty elegantly spiked by putting in this really complicated political issue into the middle of the agriculture discussions.” Other observers also expressed frustration to Carbon Brief that the group had brought CBAM into the negotiations, noting that trade measures are being discussed elsewhere in the COP.  At the end of this session, parties were asked to submit their views in writing for consideration, with the LMDCs proposing an extension of SJWA to COP32.  A draft text circulated on the evening of 12 November – after the scheduled start of the negotiations that evening – left many parties unsatisfied, with several stating that elements of the text crossed their “red lines”. The draft presented parties with four options, including “no text”. Options for SJWA presented in a draft text on 12 November. Source: UNFCCC . Although various parties objected to many parts of the proposed text – including agroecology (opposed by India), CBAM (opposed by the EU) and “food systems” language (opposed by the G77) – the underlying issue was a lack of finance, observers told Carbon Brief. Marie Cosquer , advocacy analyst at Action Against Hunger , said:  “The main issue is not bad-faith negotiating; it’s the fact that across the UNFCCC, the countries that have a climate debt are not paying it…Unless they move on finance, there is nothing in this negotiation for global south countries.” With no sight of agreement on the horizon and the scheduled negotiating time drawing to a close, parties suggested that the negotiations end with a procedural text. The co-facilitators put such a text forward on 14 November. This final text says only that parties “continued consideration” of SJWA and have “requested the subsidiary bodies to continue consideration” of SJWA at the mid-year intersessional meetings in Bonn. The subsidiary bodies are then “requested” to report back at COP32.  Mitigation work programme The “mitigation work programme” (MWP) stalled repeatedly over the two weeks of COP31, and was ultimately blocked in the closing plenary, with work pushed back to Bonn in 2027.  The MWP – the only formal agenda item at the annual COP that is specifically focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions – was set to come to an end in 2026. As such, parties have been wrangling with an existential question over the past year – both regarding the continuation of the programme and what it should work on. Both in Bonn and at COP31, divisions arose over the challenge of ensuring the MWP is “facilitative and non-prescriptive and…drive[s] greater urgency on mitigation ambition and implementation”, as the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions noted . At the Bonn intersessional meetings in June, countries were unable to agree on how to balance these two aspects and negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning there was no outcome and discussions were knocked over to the next session.   In the run-up to COP31, submissions from parties made it clear that there was support for the continuation of the programme.  According to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB), as negotiations got underway on 10 November, parties diverged on the duration of the programme – with suggestions including out to 2030 or 2040 – and on a review of the purpose of MWP.  Additionally, Switzerland proposed establishing a permanent mitigation committee that would be similar to standing bodies in other areas of the UNFCCC process. This was opposed by the Arab group. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Speaking to Carbon Brief, Lola Vallejo , diplomacy and partnerships director at the European Climate Foundation (which funds Carbon Brief) and former co-chair of the MWP, said the proposal raised an “interesting question”.  She noted that, alongside the climate finance “work programme”, there is a standing committee focused on finance, but there has not been one proposed for mitigation previously.  Vallejo added that while finance discussions may not be “getting the political traction” many wanted at COP31, “at least there’s no shortage of spaces to discuss”, unlike mitigation, which solely has the work programme. Observers told Carbon Brief that there was pushback against this proposed mitigation committee, on the basis that there is not a lack of institutions or bodies to tackle the issue, rather, there is a lack of finance and support. Areas of divergence between parties included connection (or not) to the “ global stocktake ”, connection to NDCs or other collective goals, mentions of the IPCC and to what extent the “action agenda” can be brought in, according to Vallejo.  Various designs for the continuation of the MWP were proposed in subsequent negotiations, including multi-year work plans and introducing more “focused, solutions-oriented global dialogues” to facilitate implementation. The extent of the disagreements was evident in a draft text published at the end of the first week of COP31, which contained 177 square brackets and 12 “options”.  In the second week in Antalya, progress continued to stall in the MWP negotiations. A new draft text released on 18 November highlighted that the duration of the programme, links to the global stocktake (GST) and the potential for a committee remained contentious.  While it was cut down from the previous iteration, this was, in part, because contentious issues had been replaced by placeholders without any content, as shown below. Draft text for the MWP, published 18 November. Source: UNFCCC . Natalie Jones , senior policy advisor on energy at the International Institute for Sustainable Development , told Carbon Brief that some parties were pushing to weaken language around the MWP’s original mandate to “accelerate action in this critical decade”, as well as language linking the work programme to the GST. She said:  “Some parties want to limit what the GST can say on mitigation. Basically, they want to avoid another sort of transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) situation at COP33 and avoid any more top-down or sectoral targets or whatever, and they fear that they could come out of the MWP into the stocktake.” The next day, another draft text was published. This was close to agreement, with just two outstanding options: whether the MWP should take into account any “mitigation-related outcomes” of each stocktake when planning its activities or dialogues, or to have no text on the matter.  The draft text “decides” that one global dialogue will be held every year from 2028 under the MWP, leaving the door open for additional in-person or hybrid dialogues. Furthermore, it decides that the work programme will be extended until the end of 2030 and be renamed the “Sharm el-Sheikh-Antalya mitigation ambition and implementation work programme”.  Speaking to Carbon Brief, Fernanda de Carvalho , head of policy for climate and energy at WWF International , said the continuation of the MWP would be “better than nothing”, but added the process needed to be “significantly strengthened to deliver on its mandate”.   She added:  “A few parties keep pretending the link between this process and the GST doesn’t exist; they should just look at the decision that created the MWP.” Despite a clean text being released on 21 November – with the reference to the Paris Agreement removed from the preamble, but the reference to the GST remaining – parties failed to adopt the MWP in the closing plenary. Saudi Arabia and Russia both rejected the programme there, with the former stating it was “deeply disappointed by the continued attempts throughout these negotiations to fundamentally alter the facilitative, non-prescriptive and bottom-up nature of the mitigation work programme”. It said parties had tried to “move it away from its agreed mandate”. The UK, for the Umbrella group, lamented that the MWP could not be agreed, adding that the “complementarity of the global stocktake has been part of the MWP mandate from the beginning”. With no agreement in Antalya, work on the MWP will be pushed to Bonn in 2027, with the future of the programme uncertain. Response measures Talks on “response measures” were some of the least contentious at COP31, however, the final plenary still rejected a draft decision on the topic.  At UN climate talks, “ response measures ” is a forum for discussing the effects of carbon-cutting policies on countries. They are particularly relevant for nations where controls on emissions or deforestation pose a risk to communities and the economy.  In recent years, the forum has been where trade and climate issues have been discussed.  In 2024, COP29 in Baku established a four-year work plan on response measures, including the “cross-border impacts” of climate-change measures. This created a formal space to discuss and assess trade-related climate measures in UN climate talks.  COP30 in Belém established a two-day “global dialogue” on response measures each year from 2026-29. The first was in Bangkok from 21-22 September 2026, focusing on economic diversification and on how to manage impacts on vulnerable populations. COP31 also conducted its first annual ministerial high-level round table on response measures on 17 November. Credit: Kubilay Ciftci / UNFCCC In Antalya, three key disputes emerged. The first was on what activities the forum would undertake in 2027 and, second, how it would consider recommendations from its Katowice Committee (KCI) of experts. The third was on whether – and how – response measures would inform the second “ global stocktake ”. At the start of negotiations, countries – including the African group, AOSIS, South Korea and China – called for a wide range of activities next year. One of these included a new “cross-border” impact assessment of response measures. On 16 November, the EU suggested removing an activity that refers to Article 3.5 of the 1992 UN climate convention, covering trade and an “open international economic system”.  Eventually, countries settled on four different activities. These include a workshop next June for the most affected countries to learn how to report these impacts, plus another workshop at COP32 on “technological solutions” to reduce climate impacts. As work on the second global stocktake (GST2) gets underway, countries disagreed on how response measures would feed into it. As of 19 November , the same four options remained on the table, including one with “no text”.  One option, supported by G77 and China, “decide[d]” that all of the outputs of the forum – dialogues, workshops, technical reports and case studies – would serve as substantive inputs to GST2.  This option “urged” that the cross-border impact assessment be conducted “before and during” GST2, including metrics such as inflation, trade flows, household income, employment and debt. Canada and the EU warned that this would change the global stocktake’s “well-established function”, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  However, Switzerland, Norway, EU and the UK supported a compromise option – where countries could submit their views on the “social and economic impacts of response measures” as input to GST2.  Eventually, the option explicitly containing a cross-border impact assessment as an input to  GST2 was deleted from the final draft .   Instead, the text “recognises” that inputs to GST2 are “non-exhaustive” and “affirms” that all the forum’s outputs will feed into the stocktake’s technical assessment. This includes work on cross-border impacts – including trade measures – and how to report and analyse them. At the same time, it “invites” countries to submit their views on the “social and economic consequences” of response measures by 28 February 2027, which would also inform the stocktake. During the final plenary, the EU told delegates it objected to the adoption of the decision on response measures, on the grounds that it “contains provisions that are highly problematic”, as well as “the lack of recognition of the best available science”.  This was supported by Canada and the UK, with the latter adding: “We cannot accept any outcome that seeks to undermine and unduly influence the next global stocktake.” Brazil and Saudi Arabia both expressed their disappointment with the rejection of the text. Brazil said that the draft “excludes the voices of developing countries, the very countries that struggle to address the social and economic impacts of mitigation measures”. It asked for a formal note that the role and mandate of the forum were being “undermined”. Action for climate empowerment A draft decision on “ action for climate empowerment ” (ACE) had been set for adoption at COP31, but was unexpectedly torpedoed by Russia in the closing plenary. This area of the negotiations aims to encourage people to engage in climate action in different ways – through education, training, public awareness and access to information. COP27 had agreed to a four-year “action plan” on ACE that ends this year. COP31 was due to have agreed a new plan for 2027-2031, with some parties wanting it to address “misinformation and disinformation” related to climate change. During the Antalya talks, Russia, along with Saudi Arabia and Paraguay, objected to including a reference to countering climate-related “misinformation and disinformation”, reported ENB . It added that Russia described this as amounting to the censorship of other scientific views. Russia also made repeated efforts to replace previously agreed language on “gender-responsive” action with the phrase “gender-sensitive”. A draft decision , proposed by the presidency on 21 November, “note[d] the need to enhance efforts to promote and support the integrity of information on climate change”. The proposal also “recognise[d] the centrality of equity and the best available science for effective climate action and policymaking, as provided by the IPCC”. It then set out an action plan for continued work from 2027-2031. Notably, while references to “misinformation” had been removed, it still talked of “ensuring that the public has access to reliable, accurate climate information and is equipped with adequate climate literacy skills”. Draft text for the ACE “action plan”, published 21 November. Source: UNFCCC . During the closing plenary, however, Russia said it “reject[ed]” the “censorship of science” and that it “objected” to the draft text on action for climate empowerment. It said discussions had been “held hostage by considerations which are not part of the climate process”. The EU and the UK for the Umbrella group expressed their “surprise” at Russia’s objection. The UK said this topic was “very important for our group” and that “respect for gender equality and all identities is core to an effective, inclusive and meaningful process”. The COP president told the plenary that, “in light of the objection from the Russian Federation”, the issue of action for climate for empowerment would be deferred until the Bonn talks in June 2027. In a statement, campaign group Climate Action Against Disinformation said: “The ACE action plan should have been a milestone for truth at COP31. Instead, the Russian federation – the epicentre of climate disinformation – blocked its adoption, standing alone against 193 other[s].” Trade After the creation of three annual “dialogues” on trade within the COP30 Belém “global mutirão” decision, the topic was not expected to feature on the official agenda, even if it was likely to come up in other negotiating tracks. But, in the end, the rejection of not only the cover decision, but also agreements on “response measures” and agriculture, meant that trade was entirely missing from the COP31 outcome. (See: Response measures and Agriculture .) (A request from the African group to add trade to the COP31 agenda was also rejected .) Trade and climate featured strongly in the first “ reflections ” text on a cover decision, which was a compilation of suggestions from parties. Paragraph 119 of the first draft “call[ed] on” developed countries to “phase out unilateral…trade-restrictive measures” by the end of 2027. Commonly cited examples of what this might refer to include the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism and deforestation law. (See: Agriculture and food security .) First draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC The phase-out call was, expectedly, cut from the second iteration of the cover text.    Speaking to Carbon Brief, global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia Yao Zhe said: “No one thought it would survive, probably even the ones [who] proposed it. But I see it as an indication that [countries] are persistent in pushing the trade angle.” Yao added that she expected China, with the African group, to “aim for higher” on trade at next year’s COP32 summit. In the end, with the “Antalya pact” failing, none of the references to trade survived the conference. In the closing plenary, Russia, Venezuela, Brazil, Iran, Kenya – with the Arab and African groups – lamented how the issue of trade was treated in the talks, with Saudi Arabia saying developing countries were told “this is a matter that is completely off the table”. Russia’s representative remarked that “climate policy should not turn into trade policy by other means”, calling customs tariffs on “green” supply chains “old colonial distribution of labour under a new green banner.” Ghana, for the African group, pointed out “no firm treatment” of trade measures at COP31. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Ghana and Kenya both flagged the lack of “firm treatment” of trade measures and hinted that it would be a priority for them at COP32. Kenya’s delegate said: “Unilateral trade measures are only noted. African economies bear their costs, while the decision merely notes their views.”  Second global stocktake Against a backdrop of fraught negotiations, the second “ global stocktake ” (GST) was launched at a high-level event in the middle of the second week of COP31. The GST is the Paris Agreement’s five-yearly “ reality check ”, measuring whether the world’s collective efforts are enough to sufficiently cut emissions and prepare for climate impacts. The first stocktake culminated in Dubai at COP28 in 2023, resulting in the first-ever global commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels ”, among various other pledges. GST2 will run until 2028, meaning COP33 will have to address the likely shortfall between the Paris Agreement’s goals and reality. An important question hanging over this process is whether parties will have access to the latest IPCC science in time for the second GST, as a small group of countries push for the next IPCC report to be published after the stocktake. (See: Cover text. ) COP31 also featured a “dialogue” on how the lessons of the first GST could inform countries’ future NDCs.  Parties such as the EU and climate-vulnerable nations argued for a more substantial outcome that included guidance for the second GST and references to the 1.5C target. This was opposed by many developing countries. In the end, parties decided on a procedural outcome without any of the more ambitious language that had appeared in previous drafts . Long-term goal review COP31 was unable to agree on whether to start a third “periodic review” of the UN climate convention ’s long-term goal and progress towards meeting it. The goal of the 1992 convention is to avoid “dangerous” climate change, a target that was defined at COP16 in 2010 as a warming limit of 2C. COP16 also said that this goal – and progress towards meeting it – should be subject to “periodic review”. The first review , in 2013-2015, helped secure the Paris 1.5C limit. At the start of the second review at COP25 , some parties disputed the need for the process, given the existence of five-yearly “ global stocktakes ” of progress under the Paris Agreement. Underlying this disagreement is the fact that the convention has distinct country requirements for developed and developing parties, whereas the Paris regime does not. Discussions on a third review stalled at COP29 and continued at COP30. Some developed countries said it was “ redundant ”, while developing countries wanted it to continue. In Antalya, countries were split over whether to begin a third periodic review, whether to delay it until publication of the next IPCC report, or whether to discontinue the process. The final COP31 text “notes the consideration” of the matter and decides to continue talking at COP32 next year. At the first closing plenary , China, along with India for the LMDCs and Saudi Arabia for the Arab group, expressed their “concern” over the lack of agreement. China said: “We are seriously concerned that some developed country parties…in the name of streamlined process…substantively tried to terminate this mechanism.” For AOSIS, Palau “regret[ted]” the lack of progress on what it said was the “only dedicated space to reflect on the 1.5C limit on the basis of substantive scientific input”. Guidance on NDCs COP31 was unable to agree on further guidance for countries when preparing their climate pledges under the Paris Agreement, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). This issue has been disputed in the past, with talks also failing at COP29 in Baku two years ago. In Antalya, parties were once again split over whether to issue further guidance Developed and vulnerable countries – including the EU and small island states – want more guidance, to prompt stronger implementation and more transparent pledges. The LMDCs, the Arab group and African group, prefer to avoid what they see as prescriptive further guidance that could impinge on the “nationally determined” nature of the documents. The negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning they ended without agreement and will resume at the next session of the talks in Bonn next June. Rio synergies To the dismay of many countries, negotiations on the need for “synergies” between the three Rio conventions of climate change, biodiversity loss and land desertification ended with the adoption of just a one-line text .  The text simply states that, during negotiations under this item – known as “cooperation with other international organisations” – there was an “exchanges of views” and an agreement to “continue consideration at the next session”. The agreed text for the “cooperation with other international organisations” agenda item. Source: UNFCCC . On 10 November – the second day of COP – ENB reported that Russia, supported by the Arab group, “opposed continuing the discussion” on Rio synergies. Speaking on the behalf of 14 small island developing states in plenary on 14 November, Fiji said it was “deeply disappointed” by the outcome. It told delegates: “We came to Antalya ready to advance cooperation across Rio conventions and to foster synergies in national implementation. That is what all parties agreed to do when we left Bonn . We did not do that. Not because the issues were too difficult, but because we were never permitted to discuss them in the way we intended to do so. “At the very first informal consultation, before a single substantive proposal had been heard, the intention to invoke ‘ rule 16 ’ was announced by one group of party. We offered repeatedly to address any and all concerns. That offer was not taken up. Substantive discussion was blocked from the very first hour to the last.” The EIG, Panama for AILAC, the UK for the Umbrella group and the EU all expressed similar disappointment. Around the COP Fossil fuels The issue of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” dominated again at COP31, with countries leaving the talks still deeply divided on how it should be taken forward. Including “transitioning away from fossil fuels” in the cover decision was one of the key asks of a group of 126 countries spanning Europe, the small island states, parts of Latin America and the Caribbean and other major developed countries. In the end, several countries rejected the proposed cover decision over its lack of a clear reference to fossil fuels, with the EU saying: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” Fossil fuels also featured prominently on the sidelines at COP, with more than 80 side events and talks dedicated to the topic, Carbon Brief understands. In addition, eight European and small island nations announced intentions to release national roadmaps away from fossil fuels – bringing the total number with such plans up to 27. The first major event on fossil fuels took place on the summit’s second day, when the Brazilian COP30 presidency formally presented its global fossil-fuel roadmap to a packed-out plenary room. Daisy Dunne 10 November 2026, 11:28 GMT Fossil-fuel roadmap presented at COP31 Hi, I’m Daisy Dunne, one of Carbon Brief’s associate editors. I’m reporting from a plenary session at COP31 in Turkey, where the Brazilian COP30 presidency has just officially presented its global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. COP30 president… Read more on CB Connect → (The COP30 presidency agreed to bring forward a voluntary roadmap after countries failed to agree to one by consensus at the Belém summit last year.) In Antalya, COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago told delegates that the roadmap is “not a mandate” and “not related to the negotiations”. Instead, he said, “it’s contribution and input for the implementation that we need to do”. The session featured key figures, including UN secretary general António Guterres, UN climate chief Simon Stiell, COP26 president Alok Sharma and former US climate envoy John Kerry. However, COP31 presidents Kurum and Bowen were conspicuously absent. The next day, during his speech at the world leaders’ summit, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called on Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in [the roadmaps] are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This included a bullet point saying some parties would like to see “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” included in the text. (This language was first agreed by countries as part of the first global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai in 2023.) On the same day, Irene Vélez Torres, Colombia’s former environment minister, told journalists that a mere repetition of language agreed in Dubai would not represent progress for many parties. Vélez Torres co-led a first-of-its-kind conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta in April this year, which was attended by 57 countries. She told the huddle that, regardless of what is agreed by consensus on fossil fuels at COP31, countries committed to transitioning away would continue to take action, saying: “Consensus as a method is not going to stop us anymore…we know it has limited ambition. It is limiting implementation, but this is not going to stop us.” On Monday 16 November, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.  One part of this draft “call[ed] for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”. Another part of the text also “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led global roadmaps on the transition away from fossil fuels and on ending deforestation. The next day, a group of European and small island state ministers held a press conference on the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Denmark, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg announced that they intend to release new national roadmaps away from fossil fuels.  (Earlier that day, Vanuatu had announced its own national roadmap and the development of a Pacific regional roadmap away from fossil fuels.)  Speaking as a united front, the group of ministers called for the language on fossil fuels contained within the first draft to be strengthened and given more prominence. However, Carbon Brief understands that, behind-the-scenes, hopes that any kind of fossil-fuel language would survive into the second draft cover decision were fast evaporating. On 18 November, a group of global-south ministers held a press conference, attended by Carbon Brief, to show their support for transitioning away from fossil fuels. At the event, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Guatemala announced that they were joining the fossil fuel treaty , an initiative to develop a legal instrument to control fossil fuels. This brought the total number of countries supporting the treaty up to 30. During the press conference, Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro made headlines with an explosive speech, telling journalists that the world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. The next day, the co-hosts of the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference – Tuvalu and Ireland – held a press conference. They confirmed that a pre-conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels would be held in Dublin in May, with the actual conference taking place in Tuvalu in July. Speaking at the press conference, Tuvalu climate minister Maina Talia publicly acknowledged he was not expecting to see transitioning away from fossil fuels in the second draft of the cover decision. The co-hosts also confirmed that a third transitioning away from fossil fuels conference will be held in 2028. (Lula told civil society at COP that Brazil was keen to host it. Carbon Brief understands Cambodia and Ghana are also interested.) Later that day, a second draft cover decision was published. It did not mention “fossil fuels” at all, nor “paragraph 28 of decision 1/CMA.5”, the passage of text from the first global stocktake that calls for countries to contribute to “transitioning away from fossil fuels”. In the evening, Kurum and Bowen held a press conference to defend their second draft and tried to bat away questions from journalists about whether the removal of fossil-fuel language represented “backsliding”. Both presidents cited their push to get countries to sign up to electrification as complementary to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with Bowen telling journalists: “The world agreed at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels. What we’re about is practical ways to do that. There’s no better way than electrification.”  However, it was widely understood that many countries were not happy with the omission of fossil fuels. The group was fronted by Netherlands climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven, who said she represented the views of Germany, France, Denmark, Panama, Brazil, Luxembourg, Ireland, the UK, Sweden, Indonesia, Iceland, Finland, Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, Portugal, Norway, Fiji and Spain. Guatemala, Belgium and Switzerland were also on the stage. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update on the state of the text failed to materialise.  Tuvalu’s Talia told a cramped press huddle that Pacific island nations had been waiting for the text since last night and were still willing to fight to get transitioning away from fossil fuels back in. Maina Vakafua Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, speaks to journalists. Credit: Sandro Basili / Alamy Stock Photo On Saturday evening, the fallout over fossil fuels intensified.  Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UG, AOSIS, AILAC and LDCs – approached the presidency as a united front to demand that transitioning away from fossil fuels featured in the final cover decision. One observer told Carbon Brief that such close cooperation between the EU and AOSIS is “unprecedented” at COP. They added that it might reflect the fact that Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, is working closely with Tuvalu on holding the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference next year. A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  This one also did not directly mention fossil fuels. However, it did “recall” the COP28 UAE consensus “in its entirety”, which itself includes a reference to a “just, orderly and equitable” transition away from fossil fuels. Carbon Brief contributing editor Dr Joanna Depledge wrote on LinkedIn that this oblique reference was “near meaningless”. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, many countries rejected the text – citing its failure to clearly reference transitioning away from fossil fuels as one of the key reasons. (See: Cover decision .) Action agenda Many issues that were intensely negotiated at COP31 – including the electrification goal and fossil-fuel phaseout – also featured in the “ action agenda ”. This is the part of the UN climate process that involves mobilising real-world climate action from non-state actors, including businesses, investors and civil-society groups.  It also covers voluntary actions taken by groups of countries beyond the COP negotiations. When the “Antalya pact” failed to materialise, the presidency’s action agenda package was one of its more substantial outputs.  In this closing remarks at COP31, after the headline negotiated outcome had collapsed, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell reminded delegates: “This COP process has two tracks. And across the action agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.” With Australia overseeing negotiations, the action agenda was instead a priority for the Turkish presidency, which used COP31 to launch a variety of new projects and “ compacts ”. In a phrase familiar to attendees of previous COPs , Turkish COP31 president Murat Kurum said he wanted an “implementation COP” that would leave people saying: “Something changed in Antalya.” Delegates resting by a wall with the COP31 slogan “dialogue, consensus, action”. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Amid global conflict, struggling multilateralism and the imminent breaching of the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal, UN climate talks have repeatedly failed to reach consensus on vital issues. Some have, therefore , welcomed what the Brazilian COP30 presidency called “two-tier multilateralism”, in which parties try to find consensus where they can and, where they cannot, coalitions of willing nations and groups push more ambitious action forward. Kaveh Guilanpour , vice president for international strategies at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), told Carbon Brief: “There’s a lot of inertia in the formal way of negotiating and we’re trying to find our way to whatever that new thing is, given the foundational era of negotiations is over.” Last year, the Brazilian presidency consolidated hundreds of existing climate initiatives – including many launched at previous COPs – into a streamlined set that could be supported and tracked under the action agenda. This included setting out more than 120 “ plans to accelerate solutions ”, to advance everything from phasing out coal to ending food waste. Tracking by UN Climate Change found that 104 of these plans had seen progress over the past year. By the end of COP31, the total number of plans had increased to 136, with new ones filling “ important gaps ”, such as early warning systems . Crucially, the plans were structured to align with the global stocktake outcomes from COP28 – such as curbing fossil fuels and tripling renewables – which all nations agreed on.  In this way, the revised action agenda is intended to explicitly support negotiated outcomes. Turkey announced 10 “ priority themes ” for the COP31 action agenda, fitting them into the existing framework. By far the most high profile was the “electrification” focus. (See: Electrification .) A book distributed at the summit by the Turkish presidency stated that a “large number of events, declarations and partnerships does not by itself constitute implementation success”. Nevertheless, the presidency did launch many new initiatives, including six voluntary 2035 targets that countries and non-state actors could sign up for.  These included “compacts” to curb the “ energy intensity ” of buildings by 25% and increase the use of “circular materials” in manufacturing to at least 15% by 2035. These initiatives attracted dozens of backers, but gained far less support than the electrification goal. Other notable initiatives pushed by the Turkish presidency include a domestic pledge for “ zero waste districts ” and an “ Antalya artificial intelligence (AI) pledge ”, which focused on curbing data-centre emissions while advancing “AI solutions for climate action”. COP31 also saw progress on two initiatives launched by COP30’s “ global mutirão ” decision that are relevant for the growth of the action agenda. The first was the “ Belém mission to 1.5 ”, which identified key priority areas for countries to meet their climate goals.  The second was the “ global implementation accelerator ”, which was formally established at COP31. This involves presidencies and experts choosing two action-agenda plans each year that are best placed to drive “ positive tipping points ” for climate action.  Cosima Cassel , E3G climate diplomacy lead, told Carbon Brief that this focus, “based on science, not just on the presidency’s priorities…is an extra step in the evolution of the action agenda”. Global climate action high-level event. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . During a COP31 session on the “accelerator”, COP30 strategy director Túlio Andrade said the Brazilian team wanted it to advance the transition “from a negotiation-focused regime to one very much focused on implementation”. The Turkish presidency also announced a new project called the “ climate implementation bridge ”, while pledging an initial $3m to support its operations. In partnership with the UN Development Programme, the bridge’s goal is to turn nations’ climate plans into “ bankable projects ” and connect them with finance.  Together, the “mission”, “accelerator” and “bridge” form part of a wider “ ecosystem ” that supporters hope will identify and support priority areas of climate action. However, the growing profile of the action agenda has resulted in pushback, with India and the Arab group arguing against any mention of it in formal negotiations. In contrast, Brazil accused the presidency of failing to significantly acknowledge these “concrete instruments and initiatives” in the proposed “Antalya pact”.  Some parties and observers are concerned that the action agenda is a diversion from parties’ obligations under UN climate treaties, such as providing climate finance. Arguing that the focus should instead be on reforming the COP process, Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu told Carbon Brief: “Unfortunately, the action agenda has not necessarily led to action. It is indicative, again, that the COP process is broken. While people innovating and coming together to take action is good, it cannot take the place of negotiations.” Developing countries, which often have far fewer delegates , also struggle to follow all the additional activities. In a closing session , Stiell invited parties to nominate focal points so that the UN could help to “connect them with action agenda opportunities all year round”. Guilanpour noted that while “everybody says they want to focus on implementation”, within the traditional COP process this can only apply to “a very rarefied subset of obligations”, such as submitting revised NDCs. He added: “When the rest of the world hears implementation, they want to see pollution in their city going down, their energy bills going down…and that sort of implementation is in the action agenda.” Global leaders COP31’s world leaders’ summit took place during the conference’s first week from 11-12 November. Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – whose recent re-election was widely interpreted as a timely boost for climate action and multilateralism by delegates – gave a blistering speech in the summit’s opening ceremony. He told other world leaders: “We have started talking more about weapons and tariffs than about the survival of future generations…But the planet cannot be left at the mercy of hegemonic disputes.” He told leaders that he wanted COP30 , which took place last year in the Brazilian city of Belém, to be remembered as the “COP of truth” – but that “science and multilateralism remain under attack”, adding: “It is not by chance that the incorporation of IPCC contributions into the COP negotiation process is in question. Nor is it a coincidence that climate agreements are the favourite targets of reactionary forces at COPs.” He also touted Brazil’s newly released global roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation , urging COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in these documents are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. In one of his final addresses in the role, UN secretary general António Guterres said that the “brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us”, adding: “Leaders – and, in particular, those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil-fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.” Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdoğan used his address to call on developed countries to “take greater responsibility for emission reductions and financing” and to call out “ecocide” in Gaza. (Erdoğan faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields in Turkey on the eve of the summit.) Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley cited Carbon Brief analysis to reprimand developed countries in her address to the world leaders’ summit, telling the room: ”My friends, let us be clear: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.” UK prime minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the summit, said that electrification is “how we make clean power cheap power”. He also announced the appointment of the country’s first special representative on climate security.  In total, around 70 world leaders spoke at the summit – with many major polluters missing. For the second year, the US did not send any delegates to COP. (Donald Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and the UN climate treaty after returning to office.) However, success for Democrats in the US midterm elections, shortly before COP31, lifted hopes that the world’s second-largest emitter could one day return to the talks. “America is all in” – a coalition of mostly Democratic governors, Congress members and local mayors – had a pavilion at COP31 and brought around 120 delegates (a figure larger than many official country delegations ). Speaking on 16 November at a pavilion event attended by Carbon Brief, Jared Huffman , a Democratic Congressional representative from California, said that the midterm results were a “clear rejection” of Trump’s “climate denial” and “wrecking ball to climate and energy policy”. He added: “The next time that we are here at a COP, it will be different…We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives. And soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change and the US will truly be officially back in as part of the negotiati[ons].” Other countries without delegations at the talks included Myanmar and Israel, according to Carbon Brief analysis. More than 92,000 registered for COP, making it potentially the largest in history, found Carbon Brief analysis. Overall totals for delegates from parties, observers and the media for all COPs, as published by the UNFCCC (see this article for more details on the data). Data for COPs 1-30 are the “final” figures, while COP31 data is “provisional”.
